lessons.summary: Express, Fastify and Hono all sit on the same two objects: an IncomingMessage that is a readable stream and a ServerResponse that is a writable one. This sector is the layer they hide - header casing and multiplicity, framing a body with content-length or chunked encoding, what a 204 may not contain, what happens when a socket dies mid-write, and the four timeouts that decide whether a slow client can hold a connection open forever.

# V3·NB1 — The server under the framework

You have already written raw `node:http` handlers in `08_http_core` and drilled
them in `d18_http_raw`: routing by pathname, reading a query string, answering a
conditional GET. That work treated `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` as a
pair of objects with convenient methods. This sector treats them as what they
actually are — a readable stream and a writable stream wrapped around one TCP
socket, with a small state machine deciding what may still be written.

The reason to care is not purity. It is that every framework leaks this layer
the moment something goes slightly wrong. A response that "sometimes" has the
wrong `content-length`, a `set-cookie` that overwrites the previous one, a 204
that a proxy refuses to forward, a request that hangs for five minutes because
nobody configured `requestTimeout` — none of those are framework bugs. They are
HTTP framing rules that the framework faithfully passed through.

## The two objects

`http.createServer((req, res) => { ... })` gives you:

- `req: IncomingMessage`, a `Readable` whose chunks are the request body. Its
  `method`, `url`, `httpVersion` and `headers` come from the parsed request
  line and header block. `req.url` is the **request target**, not a URL: for a
  normal request it is origin-form, `/orders?page=2`, with no scheme and no
  host. That is why `new URL(req.url, "http://localhost")` is the standard
  incantation — you are supplying the base the wire did not carry.
- `res: ServerResponse`, a `Writable` whose chunks are the response body, plus
  a header block that has not been sent yet and a status line that has not been
  chosen yet.

The header block is the interesting half, because it exists in two states.
Before the first byte of the response goes out, headers are mutable: you can
`setHeader`, `getHeader`, `removeHeader`, `appendHeader`. The moment anything
is written — `writeHead`, `write`, `end`, or `flushHeaders` — they are frozen
and sent. `res.headersSent` tells you which world you are in, and any code that
might run late (an error handler, a `finish` listener, a timing wrapper) has to
check it before touching a header. Setting a header after the fact throws
`ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`, and in a request handler that throw usually arrives
somewhere useless.

## Header names are lowercase, and that is a decision

`req.headers` is a plain object whose keys have been lowercased for you,
because HTTP field names are case-insensitive and Node normalises rather than
making every caller do it. `req.rawHeaders` keeps the original spelling and the
original order as a flat array of alternating names and values — the only place
to look when you are debugging a signature scheme that hashes the literal
bytes, or a proxy that cares about order.

Repeated fields are where the object shape gets lossy. Node's rule is per-field
and worth memorising rather than deriving: `set-cookie` is always an array; a
handful of fields that cannot legally repeat (`content-length`,
`authorization`, `user-agent`, `from`, `referer`, ...) keep only the **first**
occurrence; everything else is joined with `", "`. So `x-forwarded-for: a` plus
`x-forwarded-for: b` reaches you as the single string `"a, b"`, which is
indistinguishable from one header a client sent with a comma in it. That
ambiguity is not Node's fault — it is baked into HTTP's list syntax — but it is
the reason proxy-header parsing in sector 6 is fiddlier than it looks.

## Framing: how the other end knows you are done

A response body needs a length or a terminator, and there are exactly three
possibilities on HTTP/1.1:

1. **`content-length: N`** — the receiver reads N bytes. Cheapest, and required
   if you want the client to show a progress bar.
2. **`transfer-encoding: chunked`** — each chunk is preceded by its size in
   hex, and a zero-length chunk ends the body. This is what Node picks
   automatically when you `write()` without having set a length.
3. **Close-delimited** — the body ends when the connection does. HTTP/1.0
   behaviour, and it costs you connection reuse.

Node picks for you: `res.end("hi")` with no headers set computes a length;
`res.write(a); res.write(b); res.end()` goes chunked. Both are correct. What is
not correct is setting a `content-length` that disagrees with the bytes you
write — Node will truncate or error, and a proxy in between may do something
worse. Compute lengths with `Buffer.byteLength(body)`, never `body.length`, or
the first non-ASCII character in a JSON payload silently breaks the response.

Some statuses have no body at all: 204, 304, and any response to a `HEAD`.
Node knows this and will suppress a body you try to write, but it will not
invent the headers a good 304 needs, and it will happily let you send
`content-length: 0` on a 304 where the correct move is to echo the validators.

## Sockets are not obliged to stay

Two more facts that only show up in production. First, the client can go away
mid-response: the socket errors or closes, `res.write` returns without helping
you, and any work you queue afterwards is wasted. `res.on("close")` fires in
both the normal and the abnormal case; `res.writableEnded` distinguishes them.
Second, an idle connection costs a file descriptor, so Node has four timeouts
that exist precisely to stop a slow or malicious client from holding one:
`server.headersTimeout`, `server.requestTimeout`, `server.keepAliveTimeout` and
`server.timeout`. Their defaults changed in Node 18 to close a real slowloris
hole, and knowing which one covers which phase is a standard interview
question — you will encode them in exercise 8.

Eight problems, then a challenge that puts a small correct server together and
a review on request targets. No framework, no dependencies beyond `node:http`,
`node:stream` and `node:url`. Every problem exports a factory so the gate gets
a fresh handler with fresh state, and supertest is handed the handler directly,
so nothing binds a port.

# Reading - node/v3nb01_http_server_core

Notes on the layer under the framework: the objects, the framing rules, and the
failure modes that only appear when a real network is involved.

## Notes

**`req.url` is a request target, not a URL.** RFC 9112 defines four forms:
origin-form (`/a?b=c`, what you almost always get), absolute-form
(`http://host/a`, what a proxy receives and what a client may legally send),
authority-form (`host:443`, only for `CONNECT`) and asterisk-form (`*`, only
for `OPTIONS`). Node hands you the bytes as they arrived. A server that assumes
origin-form and does `new URL(req.url, base)` will silently ignore the base
when the client sends absolute-form, because the absolute URL wins — which is a
routing bypass if your prefix checks ran on `req.url` as a string.

**`writeHead` and `setHeader` are not the same tool.** `setHeader` mutates the
pending header block and can be read back with `getHeader`. `writeHead(status,
headers)` merges its argument over that block and *sends*. So the pattern that
composes is: middleware uses `setHeader`, the final handler uses `writeHead`
for the status. Mixing them the other way — `writeHead` first, `setHeader`
after — throws. And `writeHead` returns `res`, which is why the chained
`res.writeHead(200).end(body)` reads nicely.

**`appendHeader` exists since Node 18 and solves `set-cookie`.** Two calls to
`setHeader("set-cookie", ...)` replace; two calls to `appendHeader` accumulate.
Before it existed, everyone wrote `res.setHeader("set-cookie",
[...existing, cookie])`, which is what you still fall back to when the value
might already be a string rather than an array.

**Content-length must be a byte length.** `"café".length` is 4;
`Buffer.byteLength("café")` is 5. A wrong length is not a cosmetic bug: too
small truncates the body, too large leaves the client waiting for bytes that
never arrive until a timeout fires. The safe habit is to build the body as a
`Buffer` once and use `buffer.length`.

**Reading a body is stream work, and streams need limits.** `for await (const
chunk of req)` is the modern spelling, and it gives you backpressure for free.
What it does not give you is a cap: a client that streams a gigabyte will make
you buffer a gigabyte. Every body reader in a real service checks
`content-length` first (a cheap rejection), then counts bytes as they arrive
(the honest check, because `content-length` is absent under chunked encoding),
and destroys the request when the cap is exceeded.

**Responding early to a large upload is a trap with a fix.** If you send a 413
and end the response while the client is still uploading, the client may see a
connection reset before it reads your status. The mitigation is to set
`connection: close`, respond, and destroy the socket after the response has
flushed — or, better, to advertise the limit and let `Expect: 100-continue`
clients ask first.

**`res.on("close")` is the universal cleanup hook.** It fires when the response
is finished *or* the underlying connection died. `res.writableEnded` is `true`
only in the first case. Any per-request resource — a timer, an upstream
fetch's `AbortController`, a database cursor — should be released there, not in
a `finish` listener, or an aborted request leaks it.

**The four timeouts, in the order a request meets them.** `headersTimeout`
(default 60s) bounds the time from the first byte to the end of the header
block — the slowloris defence. `requestTimeout` (default 300s, and 0 before
Node 18) bounds the whole request including the body. `keepAliveTimeout`
(default 5s) bounds how long an idle connection is kept for reuse after a
response. `server.timeout` (default 0, off) is socket inactivity. There is one
ordering rule people get wrong: `headersTimeout` is measured relative to the
connection, and it must be greater than `keepAliveTimeout` or a reused
connection can be cut before its next request arrives.

**Behind a load balancer, `keepAliveTimeout` must exceed the balancer's idle
timeout.** Otherwise there is a race: the balancer sends a request onto a
connection Node has just decided to close, and the client sees a 502 with no
log line on your side. This is the single most common "mystery 502" in Node
deployments, and the fix is one number.

**`Expect: 100-continue` is the polite version of a body limit.** A client that
sends the header pauses before the body and waits for a `100 Continue`. Node
surfaces this as a `checkContinue` event on the server *instead of* `request`,
and if you register a listener you must call `res.writeContinue()` yourself or
answer with a final status. It is the one place in HTTP/1.1 where a server can
refuse a two-gigabyte upload before a single body byte moves, and almost nobody
uses it because most clients only send the header for large bodies and some
proxies eat it.

**Trailers exist and are almost never the answer.** Under chunked encoding you
may send headers *after* the body — `res.addTrailers({ "x-row-count": "912" })`
after announcing `trailer: x-row-count`. It is the only way to report something
you learn while streaming, such as a checksum. Support is thin outside gRPC,
which uses HTTP/2 trailers as its status channel, so treat it as a thing to
recognise rather than a thing to reach for.

**Ignoring a request body does not save you the upload.** If your handler
answers without reading `req`, Node still has to drain the remaining bytes
before that connection can carry another request. Rejecting early and calling
`req.destroy()` is what actually stops the transfer.

## What each exercise is really testing

`ex1` is the header state machine and the difference between `setHeader` and
`writeHead`. `ex2` is limits on untrusted input. `ex3` is framing — the one
place where Node's automatic behaviour needs overriding. `ex4` is the lossy
header object and `rawHeaders`. `ex5` is aborted requests and the cleanup hook.
`ex6` is bodiless responses, which is where HEAD and 304 and 204 all meet.
`ex7` is writing a body larger than memory, which is `pipeline` plus
backpressure from `07_streams_2` applied to a response. `ex8` is the timeout
matrix, written as configuration rather than prose so the ordering constraints
become checkable.

The challenge is a whole small server that has to be correct on all of it at
once, and the review returns to request targets — the parsing decision that
routing, in the next sector, is built on.

# V3·NB1 — The server under the framework (archive)

## Why this layer keeps coming back

A framework is a set of defaults for the decisions in this document. When the
defaults fit, you never think about them. When they do not — a streaming
export, a signed webhook, a proxy that rewrites your headers, a client that
uploads two gigabytes — you are back here, and the fastest way to be productive
is to already know the rules.

## The response state machine

```
 headers mutable                headers sent              finished
 ----------------  write/writeHead  ------------  end()  ----------
  setHeader ok  ------------------>   body only ------->   nothing
  writeHead ok                        write ok
  flushHeaders  ------------------>
```

Three predicates tell you where you are:

- `res.headersSent` — the header block has gone out.
- `res.writableEnded` — `end()` has been called.
- `res.writableFinished` — the last byte has been flushed to the socket.

A wrapper that adds a timing header must therefore do its work *before*
anything writes, or hook `writeHead`:

```ts
function timing(res: ServerResponse): void {
  const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
  const original = res.writeHead.bind(res);
  res.writeHead = ((...args: Parameters<ServerResponse["writeHead"]>) => {
    const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - started) / 1e6;
    res.setHeader("server-timing", `app;dur=${ms.toFixed(1)}`);
    return original(...args);
  }) as ServerResponse["writeHead"];
}
```

That monkey-patch is exactly what every timing middleware in the ecosystem
does, and knowing it is a patch explains why two such middlewares fight.

## Reading a body, correctly

```ts
async function readBody(req: IncomingMessage, limit: number): Promise<Buffer> {
  const declared = Number(req.headers["content-length"]);
  if (Number.isFinite(declared) && declared > limit) {
    throw Object.assign(new Error("payload too large"), { status: 413 });
  }
  const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
  let size = 0;
  for await (const chunk of req) {
    size += (chunk as Buffer).length;
    if (size > limit) {
      req.destroy();
      throw Object.assign(new Error("payload too large"), { status: 413 });
    }
    chunks.push(chunk as Buffer);
  }
  return Buffer.concat(chunks);
}
```

Four things are load-bearing. The `content-length` check is an optimisation,
not the check — a chunked upload has no `content-length`. The running total is
the real check. `req.destroy()` stops the client from continuing to spend your
bandwidth. And the error carries a status, so the caller does not have to match
on message text.

## Framing, with worked examples

```ts
// 1. Length known: cheapest, enables progress bars and connection reuse.
const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(doc));
res.writeHead(200, {
  "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8",
  "content-length": body.length,
});
res.end(body);

// 2. Length unknown: chunked, chosen automatically because we write before end.
res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/x-ndjson" });
for await (const row of rows) res.write(JSON.stringify(row) + "\n");
res.end();

// 3. Bodiless: 204 carries no content-length at all.
res.writeHead(204).end();
```

Common mistakes:

- **`content-length: body.length` on a string.** Use `Buffer.byteLength`.
- **Setting both `content-length` and `transfer-encoding`.** That is a request
  smuggling vector when a proxy and an origin disagree about which wins; Node
  refuses the combination on requests and you should never emit it on
  responses.
- **Writing a body on 204 or 304.** Node drops it, but a `content-length`
  header you set stays and now lies.
- **Forgetting `charset=utf-8`.** For `application/json` it is technically
  redundant (JSON is UTF-8 by definition) but harmless; for `text/plain` and
  `text/html` its absence hands the decision to the client's guess.

## Bodiless responses and HEAD

`HEAD` must return exactly the headers `GET` would, including
`content-length`, with no body. The clean implementation is to run the `GET`
path and simply not write the payload:

```ts
const payload = render();
res.writeHead(200, {
  "content-type": "text/plain; charset=utf-8",
  "content-length": Buffer.byteLength(payload),
});
res.end(req.method === "HEAD" ? undefined : payload);
```

Anything that special-cases `HEAD` earlier will eventually drift from the `GET`
behaviour, and clients use `HEAD` precisely to trust those headers.

## Timeouts

| knob | default (Node 18+) | covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `server.headersTimeout` | 60000 | first byte to end of headers |
| `server.requestTimeout` | 300000 | first byte to end of request body |
| `server.keepAliveTimeout` | 5000 | idle between responses on a reused socket |
| `server.timeout` | 0 (off) | socket inactivity, any phase |

Rules of thumb: `keepAliveTimeout` strictly less than `headersTimeout`;
`keepAliveTimeout` strictly greater than your load balancer's idle timeout;
`requestTimeout` large enough for your biggest legitimate upload and no larger.
When `requestTimeout` fires, Node answers `408 Request Timeout` and closes.

## Aborts, and the resource you forgot

Every request should own a cancellation token, and the cheapest way to give it
one is three lines at the top of the handler:

```ts
const controller = new AbortController();
res.on("close", () => {
  if (!res.writableEnded) controller.abort();
});
```

Pass `controller.signal` into every `fetch`, every timer, every driver call
that accepts one. The endpoints where this pays are the expensive ones —
search, report generation, anything that fans out to three services — which are
exactly the endpoints impatient users abandon. Without it, a user who reloads
a slow page five times has five copies of the work running, and the fifth is
competing with the four nobody will ever read.

The mirror-image mistake is doing cleanup in a `finish` listener. `finish`
fires only when you ended the response successfully, so an aborted request
never runs it and whatever it was releasing leaks. `close` fires in both cases;
`res.writableEnded` tells the two apart when you need to know.

## Errors before a request exists

`clientError` is emitted when llhttp rejects bytes: a malformed request line, a
header block larger than `--max-http-header-size` (16 KB by default, and the
source of `HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW`), a socket reset mid-parse. There is no
`IncomingMessage` and no `ServerResponse`, only a socket, so the response is
raw bytes you write yourself. The default behaviour if you register no listener
is a plain `400` and a destroyed socket — adequate, but it gives you nowhere to
log from, and a service that cannot see its own malformed traffic is missing a
signal that usually means a broken client or a scanner.

## The interview answers

*"Walk me through what Node does between the socket and my handler."* The
parser (llhttp) reads the request line and header block, constructs an
`IncomingMessage` around the socket, and calls your `request` listener before a
single body byte has necessarily arrived. Your handler is invoked with headers
only; the body is a stream you may or may not read.

*"What does `res.end()` actually do?"* Ends the writable side: flushes headers
if they have not gone, writes the final chunk, writes the terminating
zero-length chunk if chunked, and then either keeps the socket for reuse
(keep-alive) or destroys it (`connection: close`). It does not close the socket
in the common case, which is why one leaked `setInterval` per request survives
the response.

*"How would you stream a 4 GB export?"* No `content-length`, chunked framing,
`pipeline(source, res)` so backpressure and error propagation are handled, and
an abort listener that destroys the source when the client hangs up.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `new URL(req.url, "http://x")` behave differently for a client that
   sends absolute-form?
2. Which header does Node always expose as an array, and why can it not join?
3. What happens if you `setHeader` after `writeHead`?
4. Give a case where `content-length` is absent from a request you must still
   bound.
5. Why is checking `content-length` alone insufficient as an upload limit?
6. What is the difference between `res.writableEnded` and
   `res.writableFinished`?
7. When does `res.on("close")` fire that `res.on("finish")` does not?
8. Why must `keepAliveTimeout` exceed the load balancer's idle timeout?
9. Which status codes must carry no body, and what happens to a
   `content-length` you set on them?
10. What framing does Node choose for `res.write(a); res.end(b)` with no
    headers set?
11. Why is emitting both `content-length` and `transfer-encoding` dangerous?
12. How do you add a response header from code that may run after the headers
    were sent?
13. Why does ignoring the body of a large POST not save you the upload?

# The shape of a Node HTTP server, and why it is that shape

## One socket, two streams, one parser

When a TCP connection arrives, Node's `net` layer hands the socket to an
`HTTPParser` — since Node 12 that is llhttp, Fedor Indutny's rewrite of the
old Joyent C parser, chosen because it is generated from a state machine
description and is therefore both faster and far easier to audit. The parser
emits callbacks as bytes arrive: request line, each header field, headers
complete, body chunks, message complete.

At *headers complete*, and not a moment later, Node constructs an
`IncomingMessage` and emits `"request"` on the server. This is the single most
consequential design decision in the whole stack, and everything else follows
from it. Your handler runs with a complete set of headers and an empty body:
you can decide to reject a request based on its `content-type`,
`authorization` or `content-length` before the client has spent a byte of
upload bandwidth. It is also why the body is a stream rather than a property —
at the moment you were called, it did not exist yet.

`ServerResponse` is the mirror image, a `Writable` whose `_write` goes to the
same socket, with an extra header block in front. Because it is a real stream,
everything from the streams sectors applies: `write()` returns `false` when the
kernel buffer is full, `drain` tells you when to continue, and `pipeline()` is
the correct way to connect a source to it because it propagates errors and
destroys both ends.

## Why headers are an object, and what that costs

`req.headers` being a lowercase-keyed object is a convenience that has been in
Node since 0.x, and it is right for 99% of code. The cost is that HTTP's data
model is a *list of name/value pairs*, not a map. Three consequences:

- Repeated fields must be flattened, and the flattening is lossy. Node's
  `_addHeaderLine` has a hard-coded list of fields where a duplicate is
  discarded (a defence against header-injection tricks where a second
  `content-length` disagrees with the first), a special case for `set-cookie`
  which becomes an array, and a default of comma-joining.
- The original casing is gone. Some signing schemes (AWS SigV4 is the famous
  one, though it lowercases too) and some legacy peers care.
- Order is gone. `req.rawHeaders` preserves both, as a flat array where even
  indices are names and odd indices are values, and `req.headersDistinct` (Node
  18.3+) gives you `Record<string, string[]>` when you want the honest shape
  without parsing `rawHeaders` yourself.

The lesson generalises past Node: whenever a protocol's data model is a list
and your language's is a map, you have inherited a set of edge cases and it is
better to know which ones than to be surprised.

## The framing rules, and the attack they enable

HTTP/1.1 message framing is where the protocol shows its age. A message body's
length is determined by, in priority order: the absence of a body for certain
statuses and methods; `transfer-encoding: chunked`; `content-length`; and
finally the connection closing. Two implementations that disagree about that
priority — say, a front-end proxy that prefers `content-length` and a back-end
that prefers `transfer-encoding` — can be made to disagree about where one
request ends and the next begins. That is HTTP request smuggling, and it is the
reason Node rejects requests carrying both headers, rejects obsolete
line-folding, and is strict about whitespace before the colon.

The practical corollaries for your own responses are small and absolute: emit
exactly one framing mechanism; never emit a length you have not measured in
bytes; and let Node choose when you genuinely do not know the length, because
its choice — chunked — is the correct one.

Chunked encoding is not free. Every `res.write()` becomes a size line, the
data, and a CRLF, so writing a million one-byte rows costs a great deal of
overhead and a great many syscalls. The fix is the same as in any stream
pipeline: batch. Accumulate a few kilobytes, then write once. `cork()` and
`uncork()` exist for exactly this and are used internally by Node's own
`writev` path.

## Backpressure, applied to a response

The most common Node production incident that traces back to this sector is
memory growth on a streaming endpoint. Code looks like this:

```ts
for (const row of hugeResultSet) res.write(serialize(row));   // wrong
```

`write()` returns `false` once the socket's buffer is full, and this loop
ignores it, so every remaining row is buffered in the process. On a fast
producer and a slow client — a mobile connection downloading an export — that
is the entire result set in memory, per request.

```ts
await pipeline(Readable.from(hugeResultSet).map(serialize), res);   // right
```

`pipeline` respects `false`, waits for `drain`, and — the part people forget —
destroys the source if the response dies. Without that, an aborted download
leaves a database cursor open.

## Aborts, and the work you should not be doing

A client that navigates away, a load balancer that times out, a `fetch` whose
`AbortSignal` fired: all of them produce the same thing at your end, a socket
that closes before you finished. Node surfaces it as `"close"` on the response
(and, on the request, `"aborted"`, deprecated in favour of `"close"` plus
`req.destroyed`).

The mature pattern is to create an `AbortController` per request, abort it on
`res.on("close")` when `!res.writableEnded`, and pass its signal into every
downstream call. You get cancellation of upstream fetches, database queries
that support signals, and your own loops, all from one place. The endpoints
where this matters most are the expensive ones — search, report generation,
anything fanning out — which are exactly the endpoints impatient users abort.

## The timeouts, and the CVE that set the defaults

Before Node 18, `requestTimeout` defaulted to 0 and `headersTimeout` to 40
seconds — but `headersTimeout` was measured from the *socket*'s start, which
made it possible for a client to keep a connection alive indefinitely by
trickling body bytes. CVE-2019-15605 and its relatives pushed the project to
tighten this: Node 18 turned `requestTimeout` on with a 300-second default and
re-based `headersTimeout` per request.

The practical shape of a well-tuned server sits behind a proxy, and the numbers
have to descend: the client's timeout is longer than the load balancer's, whose
idle timeout is shorter than your `keepAliveTimeout`, which is shorter than
your `headersTimeout`. When that ordering breaks, you get intermittent 502s
that no log explains, because the connection died in the gap between two
components that both believed they were being conservative.

## When not to work at this layer

Almost always. A framework gives you routing, body parsing, content
negotiation, cookies and error handling for free, and its authors have already
fixed the bugs you are about to write. Drop to `node:http` when you are
building the framework itself, when you need a behaviour the framework
actively prevents (custom framing, a protocol upgrade, byte-exact signature
verification), when you are diagnosing a framing problem, or when the
dependency itself is the risk — a webhook receiver that must not have a supply
chain.

What you should take from the sector, even if you never write `createServer`
again, is the model: headers are mutable until they are not; a body has to be
framed; a socket can leave at any time; and every convenience API above you is
making one of those three decisions on your behalf.

## Where HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change the answer

`node:http2` replaces the framing layer entirely: bodies live in streams
multiplexed over one connection, headers are HPACK-compressed and carry
pseudo-fields (`:method`, `:path`, `:status`), and `transfer-encoding: chunked`
is forbidden because framing is the transport's job. Node's compatibility API
(`http2.createServer` with `allowHTTP1`, plus `Http2ServerRequest` /
`Http2ServerResponse`) makes most handlers work unchanged, which tells you
something useful: the *interface* in this sector outlived the protocol
generation it was designed for. The parts that do not survive are the parts
that were about HTTP/1 bytes — `rawHeaders` order, chunked encoding, connection
reuse timing — which is a fair map of what to treat as protocol-specific
knowledge rather than durable design.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — the header block, before and after

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Export two things.

`safeSetHeader(res, name, value)` sets a response header only while that is
still legal: if `res.headersSent` is true it does nothing and returns `false`,
otherwise it sets the header and returns `true`. No throwing, ever — this is
the function every late-running piece of middleware in the next sector will
call.

`createHandler()` answers `GET /echo` with `200` and a JSON body:

```json
{ "method": "GET", "pathname": "/echo", "query": { "tag": ["a", "b"], "page": "2" },
  "headerNames": 3 }
```

- `query` maps each key to a **string** when it appeared once and to an array
  of strings, in arrival order, when it appeared more than once.
- `headerNames` is the count of distinct header names on the request.
- Every response carries `x-request-id`, set with `safeSetHeader`: the
  incoming `x-request-id` when there is one, otherwise `req-1`, `req-2`, ...
  counting from 1 per handler.
- `content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8` and an exact
  `content-length`, computed in bytes.

Anything else is `404` with `{"error":"not_found"}`, the same two headers, and
its own `x-request-id`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two jobs live in this problem and they are independent. `safeSetHeader` is
three lines and is about *when* a header may be set. The handler is about
building a body and describing it accurately. Write the guard first and use it
everywhere, including the 404 path — the gate checks that the error response is
as well-formed as the success one.

## Hint 2

`URLSearchParams` already knows about repeated keys; it just does not
volunteer them. Both of these are useful:

```ts
const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost");
for (const key of new Set(url.searchParams.keys())) {
  const values = url.searchParams.getAll(key);
  query[key] = values.length === 1 ? values[0] : values;
}
```

`getAll` preserves arrival order, and the `Set` stops you from visiting a
repeated key twice.

## Hint 3

Build the body as a `Buffer` once, then let its `.length` be the
`content-length`; that removes the whole class of "the length disagrees with
the bytes" bugs without you having to remember `Buffer.byteLength`.

For the counter, remember the factory shape: state declared inside
`createHandler` before the returned function is a per-handler counter, and the
gate creates a fresh handler per test precisely so it can assert `req-1`.
Increment only when you actually generate one — an incoming id must not consume
a number.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`res.headersSent` flips the moment anything is written — `writeHead`,
`write`, `end` or `flushHeaders`. Everything before that point is mutation of a
pending block that lives in memory; everything after is bytes on a socket that
cannot be recalled. Your guard is a question about which of those two worlds
the caller is in.

## Hint 2

Node's header object is already lowercased for you, so the header count is
`Object.keys(req.headers).length` — and note what that number is *not*: it is
distinct names, so a request that sent `accept` twice contributes one. If you
count `req.rawHeaders.length / 2` you will get a different answer, and the gate
sends a duplicate header specifically to tell the two apart.

## Hint 3

A shape that keeps the two responses honest is one small helper:

```ts
const json = (res: ServerResponse, status: number, value: unknown) => {
  const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(value));
  res.writeHead(status, {
    "content-type": "application/json; charset=utf-8",
    "content-length": body.length,
  });
  res.end(body);
};
```

Note that `writeHead`'s header argument merges over anything already set with
`setHeader`, so the `x-request-id` you set earlier survives. That merge order
is the reason middleware can use `setHeader` and handlers can use `writeHead`
without coordinating.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a body you have not agreed to read

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Export `readBody(req, limit)` and
`createHandler(limit)`.

`readBody` resolves with a `Buffer` of the request body, or rejects with an
`Error` carrying `status: 413` and `code: "E_TOO_LARGE"` when the body exceeds
`limit` bytes. It must reject **before reading anything** when
`content-length` already declares too much, and it must also catch the case
where there is no `content-length` at all — count bytes as they arrive and
`req.destroy()` the moment the running total passes the limit.

`createHandler(limit)` answers `POST /notes`:

- a `content-type` whose media type is not `application/json` (parameters and
  case ignored, so `Application/JSON; charset=utf-8` is fine) → `415` with
  `{"error":"unsupported_media_type"}`;
- over the limit → `413` with `{"error":"payload_too_large","limit":<limit>}`;
- an empty body or one that will not parse → `400` with
  `{"error":"invalid_json"}`;
- otherwise `201` with `{"id":"note-1","size":<byte length of the body>}`,
  ids counting from 1, and a `location: /notes/note-1` header.

Every other method or path is `404`. All responses are JSON with an exact
`content-length`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are two limit checks and they are not redundant. The `content-length`
check is an optimisation: it lets you refuse a 2 GB upload before the client
sends the second packet. The running total is the actual enforcement, because
a chunked request has no `content-length` and a lying one is trivial to send.
Write both, and let the second be the one you would keep if you had to choose.

## Hint 2

`for await (const chunk of req)` gives you the body with backpressure handled.
The overflow branch inside it needs three statements in this order:

```ts
size += chunk.length;
if (size > limit) {
  req.destroy();                       // stop the client spending bandwidth
  throw Object.assign(new Error("payload too large"), {
    status: 413, code: "E_TOO_LARGE",
  });
}
```

Throwing inside `for await` on a stream also destroys the iterator, but the
explicit `destroy()` is what makes the intent readable and the timing tight.

## Hint 3

Media type parsing is one line and people still get it wrong: the value can be
`application/json; charset=utf-8`, so split at `;`, trim, lowercase, and
compare. Do not use `includes("json")` — `application/json-seq` and
`application/vnd.api+json` are different media types and one of them is in the
gate.

Empty body and unparseable body collapse to the same 400 on purpose:
`JSON.parse("")` throws, so if you decode the buffer and hand it straight to
`JSON.parse` inside a `try`, you get both cases from one branch.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about the order of the checks as an order of *cost*. Reading a header is
free, so content-type and declared length come first. Reading the body is
expensive, so it comes next. Parsing is cheap once you have the bytes.
Answering 415 after you have buffered a megabyte is a correct response arrived
at wastefully, and the gate times nothing — but a reviewer will notice.

## Hint 2

A detail that decides whether your 413 reaches the client at all: if you
respond and end while the client is still uploading, some clients report a
connection reset instead of your status. Real servers set `connection: close`
on the 413 for exactly this reason. The gate does not require it, but adding
it costs one line and is what you would ship.

## Hint 3

Give the error a `status` and a `code` rather than a message to match on, then
the handler is a `catch` with a single branch:

```ts
} catch (error) {
  if ((error as { code?: string }).code === "E_TOO_LARGE") {
    return sendJson(res, 413, { error: "payload_too_large", limit });
  }
  return sendJson(res, 400, { error: "invalid_json" });
}
```

That is the same design as `error.code` on Node's own errors (`ENOENT`,
`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`): message text is for humans, codes are API.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — three ways to end a body

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createHandler(rows)` takes an array of objects and
serves `GET /rows`, choosing its framing from `?mode=`:

- `mode=buffered` — one JSON array, `content-type: application/json;
  charset=utf-8`, an exact `content-length`, and **no** `transfer-encoding`.
- `mode=stream` — newline-delimited JSON, one row per line including a
  trailing newline after the last, `content-type: application/x-ndjson`, and
  **no** `content-length` (Node will choose chunked because you write before
  you end).
- `mode=empty` — `204`, no body, no `content-length`, no `content-type`.

A missing `mode` behaves as `buffered`. Any other value is `400` with
`{"error":"bad_mode","allowed":["buffered","stream","empty"]}`.

The point of the exercise is that you never set both framing headers and never
set a length you did not measure. The gate reads `content-length` and
`transfer-encoding` on every response and rejects a handler that emits both or
emits a length that disagrees with the bytes.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Decide the mode first and branch to three completely separate response bodies.
Trying to share a single "send" helper across all three is what produces a
handler that sets `content-length` on the 204: the three cases have genuinely
different header sets and deserve three pieces of code.

## Hint 2

You do not ask Node for chunked encoding; you get it by not telling Node the
length:

```ts
res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/x-ndjson" });
for (const row of rows) res.write(JSON.stringify(row) + "\n");
res.end();
```

The first `write` flushes headers, and because there is no `content-length`
Node adds `transfer-encoding: chunked` itself. Setting a length here and then
writing a different number of bytes is the bug this exercise exists to teach.

## Hint 3

For `204` the whole response is `res.writeHead(204).end()`. Do not set
`content-type` (there is no content to type) and do not set
`content-length: 0`. Node knows 204 is bodiless and will drop a body you write,
but it will not remove a header you added — so the lie would survive.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the receiver has to do in each case. With a length it reads exactly N
bytes and can show a progress bar. With chunked it reads size-prefixed pieces
until a zero-length one. With 204 it reads nothing and moves on. Your three
branches are those three contracts, and the header set falls out of the
contract rather than being decorative.

## Hint 2

`Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(rows))` once, then `body.length` as the
`content-length` and `res.end(body)`, is the whole buffered branch. The
temptation to write `JSON.stringify(rows).length` is strong and wrong the first
time a row contains a non-ASCII character: `"é"` is one UTF-16 code unit and
two UTF-8 bytes.

## Hint 3

The stream branch has one subtlety worth naming even though the gate's data is
small: writing one row per `write()` costs a chunk header per row. Real
exporters accumulate a few kilobytes and write once, or use `cork()`/`uncork()`
around a batch. Correct either way — but if you ever wonder why an NDJSON
endpoint is slower than the query behind it, this is usually why.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — the headers Node's object cannot show you

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Export `collectHeaders(req)` and `createHandler()`.

`collectHeaders(req)` reads `req.rawHeaders` — not `req.headers` — and returns:

```ts
{
  names: string[];                    // lowercased, in arrival order, duplicates kept
  all: Record<string, string[]>;      // every value for every name, in arrival order
}
```

`createHandler()` answers `GET /headers` with `200` and:

```json
{ "names": ["host", "accept", "accept"], "forwardedFor": ["203.0.113.7", "70.41.3.18"],
  "duplicated": ["accept"] }
```

- `forwardedFor` is every `x-forwarded-for` value, each split on `,` and
  trimmed, flattened in order — so two headers each carrying two addresses give
  four entries.
- `duplicated` lists, sorted, the names that arrived more than once.

The response must also set **two** cookies on one response —
`a=1; Path=/` and `b=2; Path=/` — as two separate `set-cookie` values, plus an
exact `content-length`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`req.rawHeaders` is a flat array: even indices are names, odd indices are the
matching values, and nothing has been folded or lowercased. Walk it two at a
time. That is the whole of `collectHeaders`; the interesting part is why you
are not allowed to use `req.headers`, which is that it has already thrown away
the information you are being asked for.

## Hint 2

The `x-forwarded-for` shape is deliberately nasty because reality is:

```
x-forwarded-for: 203.0.113.7, 70.41.3.18
x-forwarded-for: 150.172.238.178
```

is legal and means three hops. Node's `req.headers` would give you
`"203.0.113.7, 70.41.3.18, 150.172.238.178"`, which happens to be the right
answer here — but only because comma-joining and comma-splitting are inverses
for this particular field. Do the split yourself so the behaviour is
deliberate:

```ts
const hops = (all["x-forwarded-for"] ?? []).flatMap((value) =>
  value.split(",").map((part) => part.trim()).filter(Boolean),
);
```

## Hint 3

Two cookies on one response is `res.appendHeader("set-cookie", ...)` twice
(Node 18+). If you use `setHeader` twice the second replaces the first, which
is exactly the bug that ships a login where the session cookie silently ate the
CSRF cookie. If you want the older spelling, pass an array:
`res.setHeader("set-cookie", ["a=1; Path=/", "b=2; Path=/"])`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the question "what did the client actually send?", and notice that
`req.headers` cannot answer it. It answers "what did Node decide the client
meant" — a different and usually more useful question, but not this one. Any
time you are verifying a signature, debugging a proxy, or counting hops, you
want the raw view.

## Hint 2

Node's folding rules, so you know what you are avoiding: `set-cookie` becomes
an array; `content-length`, `authorization`, `user-agent`, `referer`, `from`
and a few others keep only the first occurrence and drop the rest; everything
else is joined with `", "`. The middle rule is a security feature — two
disagreeing `content-length` headers are a request-smuggling primitive — and it
means `req.headers` will happily hide a second `authorization` from you.

## Hint 3

A shape that keeps both outputs consistent from one pass:

```ts
const names: string[] = [];
const all: Record<string, string[]> = {};
for (let i = 0; i < req.rawHeaders.length; i += 2) {
  const name = req.rawHeaders[i].toLowerCase();
  names.push(name);
  (all[name] ??= []).push(req.rawHeaders[i + 1]);
}
```

`duplicated` then falls out of `all`: the keys whose array has length above 1,
sorted. Sorting matters because object key order would otherwise leak arrival
order into an output the gate compares by value.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — the client that left

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createSlowHandler(work)` takes an injected
`work(signal: AbortSignal): Promise<unknown>` and returns
`{ handler, stats }`, where `stats` is a live object
`{ started, completed, aborted, failed }` all counting from 0.

`GET /slow` must:

- increment `started`, create an `AbortController`, and pass its signal to
  `work`;
- abort that controller if the connection closes before the response was
  finished — and increment `aborted` exactly once when that happens;
- on success, increment `completed` and answer `200` with
  `{"result": <whatever work resolved with>}`;
- on failure, increment `failed` and answer `500` with
  `{"error":"work_failed"}` — but only if the headers have not been sent and
  the request was not aborted. A rejection caused by your own abort is not a
  failure and must not be counted or answered.

Anything else is `404`. The gate destroys the connection mid-flight and then
asserts that `stats` reads `{ started: 1, completed: 0, aborted: 1, failed: 0 }`
and that nothing threw.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reframe the exercise as resource ownership. The handler owns one cancellation
token for the lifetime of one request. Its job is to hand that token to
everything it starts and to trip it the instant the request stops being worth
finishing. Counting is just how the gate observes that you did it.

## Hint 2

Why `close` and not `aborted`: `req.on("aborted")` is deprecated precisely
because it only covers one of the ways a request ends early, and it does not
fire on the response side at all. The modern advice in Node's own docs is
`res.on("close")` plus a check of what state the response reached. Attaching
to `req` also misses the case where the request body was fully received and the
client then disappeared while waiting for your answer — which is the common
case for a slow endpoint.

## Hint 3

One subtlety the gate checks: `aborted` must increment **once**. If you attach
the same logic to both `req` and `res`, or to `close` and `error`, you will
count twice on a real socket teardown. Pick a single source of truth. And note
that `controller.abort()` is idempotent, so the guard is about your counter,
not about the controller.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — responses that may not carry a body

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createHandler(doc)` serves one JSON document at
`/doc` and has to be correct about every bodiless case.

- `GET /doc` → `200`, `content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8`, an
  exact `content-length`, `cache-control: no-cache`, and a strong `etag` of
  the form `"<base64 sha1 of the body bytes>"`.
- `HEAD /doc` → **byte-identical headers**, including `content-length`, and no
  body.
- `GET` or `HEAD` with an `if-none-match` that matches (a comma-separated list,
  or `*`) → `304` with `etag` and `cache-control` and **no** `content-type`,
  **no** `content-length` and no body.
- `DELETE /doc` → `204`, no `content-length`, no body; afterwards `GET /doc`
  is `404`.
- Any other method on `/doc` → `405` with `allow: DELETE, GET, HEAD` and a
  JSON body.
- Any other path → `404` JSON.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The way to keep `HEAD` honest is to refuse to give it its own code path.
Compute the payload and the headers exactly as `GET` would, then decide at the
last line whether to write the bytes:

```ts
res.end(req.method === "HEAD" ? undefined : body);
```

Every implementation that branches earlier drifts, and clients send `HEAD`
precisely because they want to trust that the headers match the `GET`.

## Hint 2

`createHash("sha1").update(body).digest("base64")` gives you the ETag payload;
wrap it in literal double quotes, because an unquoted ETag is not a valid one
and some caches will discard it.

For the comparison, split `if-none-match` on `,`, trim, and accept `*` as a
match for any existing resource. Weak validators (`W/"abc"`) compare equal to
`"abc"` under the *weak* comparison that conditional GET uses, so stripping a
leading `W/` before comparing is the correct behaviour here.

## Hint 3

The 304 is the response people get wrong. It must not have a body, and it must
not claim one: no `content-length`, no `content-type`. It *should* repeat the
validators and the caching headers, because the client is going to store them
alongside the cached representation it already has. Node will drop a body you
try to write on a 304, but any header you set stays — so a `content-length: 0`
you added out of habit becomes a lie a proxy may act on.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write down the four bodiless situations before you code: `204`, `304`, a
response to `HEAD`, and `1xx` (which you will not produce here). Then check
your handler against the list. Almost every bug in this area is a header that
was correct for the 200 and got copied into a response that is not allowed to
have it.

## Hint 2

State lives in the factory. `DELETE` has to change what a later `GET` sees, so
the document is a mutable local — `let current: unknown = doc` and a
`deleted` flag, or simply `let current: unknown | undefined = doc` and treat
`undefined` as gone. The gate creates one handler and issues the requests in
order against it.

## Hint 3

A useful separation, because it makes the 405 fall out for free:

```ts
const ALLOW = "DELETE, GET, HEAD";
```

...set as the `allow` header on the 405 and nowhere else. RFC 9110 requires
`Allow` on a 405 — it is the only way the client learns what to try instead —
and the header value is a comma-separated list in any order, though listing
them alphabetically makes assertions easy and diffs quiet.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — a body bigger than memory

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createExportHandler(source)` takes
`source(): AsyncIterable<unknown>` and returns `{ handler, stats }` with
`stats = { aborted, truncated, failed }`.

`GET /export.ndjson` streams the source as newline-delimited JSON:

- `content-type: application/x-ndjson`, no `content-length`;
- chunks batched: accumulate serialised lines and write once the buffer
  reaches **8192 bytes or more**, then write whatever is left at the end;
- built with `pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises` so that backpressure is
  respected and the source is destroyed when the response dies.

Failure behaviour:

- the source throws **before** any byte was written → `500` with
  `{"error":"export_failed"}` and `failed += 1`;
- the source throws **after** headers went out → you cannot change the status,
  so destroy the response and `truncated += 1`;
- the client disconnects → `aborted += 1` and nothing is written.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex7
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the client can distinguish. Under chunked framing, an export
that stops early with a well-formed final chunk is indistinguishable from a
complete one — the client sees a valid, short file and imports it. Destroying
the connection is not rudeness, it is the only signal available that says "this
data is incomplete". That is the whole reason the `truncated` branch exists.

## Hint 2

`pipeline` rejects with `ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE` when the destination goes
away, which is your abort signal. You can also detect it structurally:

```ts
if (res.destroyed || !res.writableEnded && res.closed) { stats.aborted += 1; }
```

but branching on `(error as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code ===
"ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE"` is clearer about intent and survives being read
six months later.

## Hint 3

Why batch at 8192: every `res.write()` under chunked encoding emits a size line
in hex, the payload, and a CRLF, and each one is a potential syscall. Writing
one row at a time on a million-row export is measurable overhead for zero
benefit — the client cannot use a row faster than it can read a kilobyte.
8 KB is a reasonable default because it is the neighbourhood of a stream's
default `highWaterMark` and of a typical socket buffer; the exact number
matters much less than not being 40 bytes.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — the four clocks

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Export `applyTimeouts(server, opts)` and
`attachClientErrorHandler(server)`.

`applyTimeouts(server, { proxyIdleMs, maxUploadMs })` sets Node's timeouts from
two facts you actually know — how long the proxy in front keeps an idle
connection, and how long your largest legitimate upload takes — and returns the
values it applied:

```
keepAliveTimeout = proxyIdleMs + 1000
headersTimeout   = keepAliveTimeout + 5000
requestTimeout   = max(maxUploadMs, headersTimeout + 1000)
timeout          = 0
```

Both inputs must be integers greater than 0, or throw a `RangeError` naming the
offending option. The ordering that falls out — `keepAliveTimeout <
headersTimeout < requestTimeout` — is the point: it is why the numbers are
derived rather than configured independently.

`attachClientErrorHandler(server)` registers a `clientError` listener that
writes a minimal raw response to the socket and destroys it:

- socket already destroyed or not writable → destroy and return, write nothing;
- `err.code === "HPE_HEADER_OVERFLOW"` → `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`;
- `err.code === "ECONNRESET"` → destroy, write nothing;
- anything else → `400 Bad Request`.

The bytes are literal HTTP:
`HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nconnection: close\r\ncontent-length: 0\r\n\r\n`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not being asked to invent numbers; you are being asked to encode a
dependency. Each timeout covers a phase, and the phases nest: an idle
keep-alive gap is shorter than the header-reading window, which is shorter than
the whole-request window. Deriving them makes an invalid combination
unrepresentable, which is the entire argument for the exercise.

## Hint 2

`clientError` is emitted when the parser rejects bytes before a request object
ever exists — a malformed request line, a header block over
`--max-http-header-size`, a reset socket. There is no `res` to use, so you
write the response yourself:

```ts
server.on("clientError", (err: NodeJS.ErrnoException, socket) => {
  if (socket.destroyed || !socket.writable) return void socket.destroy();
  socket.end("HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request\r\nconnection: close\r\n\r\n");
});
```

Note `socket.end(...)` rather than `write` plus `destroy`: it flushes the bytes
and then closes, which is what gives the client a chance to actually read the
status.

## Hint 3

The `ECONNRESET` case exists because it is not an error you can answer — the
peer is already gone, and writing to that socket produces a second error
event, which is how a `clientError` handler turns into a crash loop. Check it
before you write, and the whole handler stays three branches.

`content-length: 0` on those raw responses is not decoration: without it the
client has to wait for the close to know the body ended, and a proxy in the
middle may hold the connection.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two questions to keep straight while writing this. *Which clock stops a slow
attacker?* — `headersTimeout`, because a slowloris drips header bytes forever.
*Which clock stops a slow but honest client?* — `requestTimeout`, and it is the
one you must raise if you accept large uploads. Setting them backwards is a
denial-of-service hole in one direction and a broken feature in the other.

## Hint 2

The `keepAliveTimeout` rule is the one with production consequences. If Node
closes an idle connection *before* the load balancer stops using it, the
balancer will eventually send a request into a socket that is closing and
return a 502 with no matching entry in your logs. That is why the formula adds
to `proxyIdleMs` rather than subtracting: you want to be the slower of the two
to give up.

## Hint 3

Validation shape that produces useful messages:

```ts
const check = (name: string, value: number) => {
  if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value <= 0) {
    throw new RangeError(`${name} must be a positive integer, got ${value}`);
  }
};
```

Naming the option in the message is the difference between a fixable
misconfiguration and a five-minute detour into your source. Node's own
`ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE` messages follow the same pattern: what was expected, and
what arrived.

## Challenge — a small server that is correct about all of it

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createApp()` returns a handler implementing a
tiny items resource, and every rule from this sector applies at once.

State: an ordered collection of `{ id, title }`, ids `item-1`, `item-2`, ...

- `GET /items` → `200`, JSON array, exact `content-length`, `cache-control:
  no-cache`, and a strong `etag` over the response bytes. A matching
  `if-none-match` gives `304` with the `etag` and no body, no `content-length`.
- `HEAD /items` → identical headers, no body, including on the `304` path.
- `POST /items` → `application/json` only (`415` otherwise), body capped at
  **1024 bytes** (`413`, `{"error":"payload_too_large","limit":1024}`),
  unparseable → `400` `{"error":"invalid_json"}`, `{"title"}` missing or not a
  non-empty string → `422` `{"error":"invalid_body","field":"title"}`.
  Success is `201`, `location: /items/item-N`, and the created item as the
  body.
- `GET /items/:id` → the item or `404`.
- `DELETE /items/:id` → `204` with no body if it existed, `404` otherwise; the
  collection ETag must change afterwards.
- A known path with a wrong method → `405` with an accurate `allow`
  (`GET, HEAD, POST` for the collection, `DELETE, GET, HEAD` for an item).
- A method outside `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `DELETE` → `501` with
  `{"error":"not_implemented"}`.
- Every response carries `x-request-id` of `r-1`, `r-2`, ... counting from 1.
- No response ever carries both `content-length` and `transfer-encoding`, and
  no bodiless response carries a `content-length`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Resist writing one long `if` chain. Three decisions happen in order and each
one narrows the next: is the method one you implement at all (else 501); which
resource does the path name (collection, item, or nothing); does this resource
support this method (else 405 with the right `allow`). Getting that order right
is most of the marks, because a 405 on an unknown path and a 404 on a known
path are both wrong.

## Hint 2

Compute the collection body first, then the ETag from those exact bytes, then
decide between 200 and 304. Doing it in that order is what makes the ETag
change automatically after a `POST` or `DELETE` — you never have to remember to
invalidate anything, because the validator is a function of the representation.

```ts
const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify([...items.values()]), "utf8");
const etag = `"${createHash("sha1").update(body).digest("base64")}"`;
```

## Hint 3

Two places where the sector's rules bite:

- `HEAD` must reach the same `writeHead` call as `GET`. Give the collection
  and item paths a single "send this representation" function that takes the
  method and decides only at `res.end(...)` whether to write bytes.
- `x-request-id` has to be on the 304 and the 204 too. Set it with
  `setHeader` at the very top of the handler, before any branch — then the
  `writeHead` calls further down merge over it rather than replacing it, and
  you cannot forget a path.

The 501 vs 405 distinction is worth one sentence of care: 501 means *this
server does not implement that method anywhere*; 405 means *not on this
resource*. `PATCH` on `/items` is a 501 here because the app implements no
`PATCH` at all.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build it as three layers with clean boundaries: a request reader (method, path
segments, body with limits), a store (a `Map` plus a counter), and a responder
(`sendJson`, `sendEmpty`, `sendNotModified`). Almost every rule in the prompt
belongs to exactly one layer, and when a test fails you will know which file
region to open. This is also the argument for why frameworks exist — you are
building the same three layers they ship.

## Hint 2

Body reading is the only asynchronous part, so keep the handler synchronous
until it needs the body. That means the `POST` branch is the one that returns a
promise, and the routing above it stays flat and easy to read. If you make the
whole handler `async`, remember that an `async` handler's rejection is an
unhandled rejection — nobody is awaiting your request listener — so it must
have its own `catch` that answers 500.

## Hint 3

A checklist to run against your implementation before you run the gate, because
these are the ones the prompt states but the eye skips:

1. Does the `304` path still set `x-request-id`?
2. Does `DELETE` return `204` with no `content-length`?
3. Does the collection ETag differ before and after a `POST`?
4. Is `allow` different for the collection and the item?
5. Is `location` relative (`/items/item-1`) and does it point at something a
   later `GET` resolves?
6. Does a 1025-byte body get `413` and not `400`?

## Review 1 — what the request line actually said

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Export `parseRequestTarget(target, host)`, which
turns `req.url` plus the `host` header into a discriminated union. This is the
parse that every router in the next sector is built on, and the reason it is a
review rather than a one-liner is that `req.url` has four legal shapes.

```ts
type Target =
  | { form: "origin"; pathname: string; query: Record<string, string[]> }
  | { form: "absolute"; pathname: string; query: Record<string, string[]> }
  | { form: "authority"; authority: string }
  | { form: "asterisk" };
```

Rules:

- `"*"` → `{ form: "asterisk" }`.
- Starts with `/` → origin-form. Parse against `http://<host>`; `query` maps
  every key to an **array** of its values in arrival order.
- Parses as an absolute `http:`/`https:` URL → absolute-form, with the same
  `pathname` and `query` — but if its host differs from the `host` header,
  throw an error with `code: "E_HOST_MISMATCH"`.
- Matches `host:port` with no scheme and no slash → `{ form: "authority" }`.
- Anything else, or an empty target → `code: "E_BAD_TARGET"`.
- An origin-form or absolute-form target with a missing or empty `host` →
  `code: "E_NO_HOST"` (HTTP/1.1 requires it, and the pathname alone is not
  enough to name a resource).

All thrown errors are `Error` instances with `status: 400` and the given
`code`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb01_http_server_core review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Order the checks from most-specific to least, because the shapes overlap.
`*` first, then a leading `/`, then "does it parse as an absolute URL", then
the authority pattern, then failure. If you try `new URL(target)` first you
will find that `"example.com:443"` parses — as a URL with the scheme
`example.com:` — which is exactly the trap the ordering avoids.

## Hint 2

The query shape is arrays all the way down, which makes it uniform for a router
to consume:

```ts
const query: Record<string, string[]> = {};
for (const [key, value] of url.searchParams) (query[key] ??= []).push(value);
```

Iterating the `URLSearchParams` directly visits repeated keys once each, in
arrival order, so no `getAll` is needed.

## Hint 3

The host comparison needs a decision you should make deliberately: compare
`url.host` (which includes a non-default port) against the raw header, both
lowercased. `Host: example.com` versus `http://example.com/x` matches;
`Host: example.com:8080` versus `http://example.com/x` does not, and that
mismatch is meaningful — it is a request that two components would route
differently, which is where cache-poisoning bugs live.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why any of this exists. Absolute-form is what a client sends to a *proxy*,
because the proxy needs to know which origin to forward to. Authority-form
exists only for `CONNECT`, when a client asks a proxy to open a tunnel.
Asterisk-form exists only for `OPTIONS *`, meaning "tell me about the server
itself, not a resource". Once you know which client sends which, the union
stops feeling arbitrary.

## Hint 2

Security angle, which is the real reason to reject a host mismatch: if your
routing uses `req.url` as a string but your link generation or cache key uses
the `Host` header, an attacker who can get an absolute-form request through can
make those two disagree. That is the shape of host-header injection and web
cache poisoning. Rejecting the disagreement outright is cheap and closes it.

## Hint 3

Give the thrown errors a helper so the shape stays consistent:

```ts
const bad = (code: string, message: string) =>
  Object.assign(new Error(message), { status: 400, code });
```

Status on the error, code for branching, message for the log — the same
discipline as ex2. And note that every failure here is a 400, not a 404: the
request itself is malformed, so there is no resource to have failed to find.

lessons.title: V3·NB2 — Routing, and a middleware pipeline you own
lessons.summary: Every Node framework is the same two ideas: a function that turns a pathname into a handler plus parameters, and a way to wrap handlers in layers that run before and after. This sector builds both from nothing - onion composition with a next() you can only call once, pattern matching with real precedence rules, method dispatch that gets 405 and Allow right, mounting with a restored base path, and the ordering bugs that make a middleware stack behave differently on the error path.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·NB2 — Routing, and a middleware pipeline you own

The previous sector left you with `req`, `res`, and a request target you can
parse. That is enough to serve one endpoint. It is not enough to serve forty,
because forty endpoints share concerns — logging, auth, body parsing, error
formatting — and every one of those concerns wants to run around the handler
rather than inside it.

Frameworks solve this with two mechanisms that look elaborate and are not. A
**router** maps `(method, pathname)` to a handler plus extracted parameters. A
**middleware pipeline** wraps that handler in layers, each of which can act
before, after, or instead of the next. That is the whole of Express, Koa,
Fastify and Hono at the architectural level; everything else is ergonomics,
plugins, and how fast the matching is.

You are going to write both. Not as an exercise in reinvention — you should use
a framework at work — but because the bugs frameworks produce are bugs in these
two mechanisms, and they are unreadable until you have implemented them once.

## Two shapes of pipeline

There are two ways to chain middleware, and the difference decides what your
framework can express.

**Express style** passes `(req, res, next)` and calls `next()` to continue.
`next` returns immediately; the middleware's own frame is finished. If you want
to do something *after* the handler, you cannot — you have to hook `res` events
instead, which is why Express timing middleware listens for `finish` and why
Express error middleware is a magic four-argument function.

**Koa style** — the onion — makes `next` return a promise:

```ts
const timing = async (ctx, next) => {
  const started = performance.now();
  await next();                        // everything downstream runs here
  ctx.set("x-time", `${performance.now() - started}`);
};
```

Downstream is now literally nested inside your frame. `try`/`catch` around
`await next()` catches errors from anything below. `finally` releases whatever
you acquired. There is no magic arity, because an error handler is just a
middleware with a `try` in it. This is strictly more expressive, and it is why
Koa, Hono and most modern designs use it.

The cost is that everything must be `async` all the way down, and that a
middleware which forgets to `await next()` produces a response before the work
below has finished — a bug with no error message. You will write the guard for
that in exercise 1.

## Matching a path is a precedence problem

`matchPath("/users/:id", "/users/42")` giving `{ id: "42" }` is the easy half.
The half that produces real bugs is precedence: what happens when
`/users/me`, `/users/:id` and `/users/*` are all registered?

The answer every serious router lands on is that specificity beats registration
order: a static segment beats a parameter, a parameter beats a wildcard, and a
longer pattern beats a shorter one. Express, famously, does *not* do this — it
tries routes in registration order, which is why Express codebases have a
convention that `/users/me` must be declared before `/users/:id`, and why
moving a route file can change behaviour. Fastify and Hono use a radix tree
with real precedence and do not care about declaration order. Both designs are
defensible; only one of them is explainable to a new team member in a sentence.

You will implement scored precedence in exercise 4, and the scoring is the
whole idea: turn a pattern into a comparable number so that ordering is a
property of the route rather than of the file.

## Method dispatch, and the 405 nobody sends

A router that answers 404 for `POST /users` when `GET /users` exists is lying:
the resource is there, the method is not supported. The correct answer is
`405 Method Not Allowed` with an `Allow` header listing what is supported —
required by RFC 9110, not optional — and it costs you one extra lookup because
you have to distinguish "no path matched" from "path matched, method did not".

The related freebie is `HEAD`. A router that matches `HEAD` against `GET`
routes and lets the response layer suppress the body gets correct `HEAD`
behaviour for every endpoint at once, which is exactly what the previous
sector's `res.end(head ? undefined : body)` was preparing for.

## Mounting, and the path you are standing on

`mount("/api/v2", router)` lets a sub-router match `/orders` while the client
asked for `/api/v2/orders`. The mechanism is a temporary rewrite: strip the
prefix, remember it as the base path, run the sub-router, restore. Express
calls the two halves `req.baseUrl` and `req.url`, and the restoration is the
part that gets forgotten — leave the path rewritten and the middleware *after*
the mount sees a path that no longer matches what the client sent, which
produces logs that are wrong in a way nobody notices for months.

## Order is the API

The last thing worth saying before the problems is that a middleware stack is
an ordered list, and the order is a design document nobody writes down. An
authentication layer registered after the router never protects anything. A
CORS layer registered after authentication makes every browser preflight fail
with a message that mentions neither. A body parser registered above a route
that streams its request buffers a file you meant to stream.

None of those produce an error. They produce behaviour that is wrong in a way
the stack trace cannot explain, which is why "read the order first" is the
correct opening move on any unfamiliar Node service, and why the assembly step
in the challenge is graded as carefully as the pieces.

Eight problems, each a piece of the machine, then a challenge that assembles a
small framework and runs a real request through it, and a review on compiling
patterns. Nothing here imports a framework: `node:http` and `node:url` only.

# Reading - node/v3nb02_routing_pipeline

Composition, matching, precedence, and the ordering rules that make a stack
behave the same on the error path as on the happy path.

## Notes

**`compose` is eight lines and worth memorising.** The canonical
implementation, from Koa:

```ts
function compose(middlewares) {
  return (ctx) => {
    let last = -1;
    const dispatch = (i) => {
      if (i <= last) return Promise.reject(new Error("next() called twice"));
      last = i;
      const fn = middlewares[i];
      if (!fn) return Promise.resolve();
      return Promise.resolve(fn(ctx, () => dispatch(i + 1)));
    };
    return dispatch(0);
  };
}
```

The index guard is not defensive decoration. Calling `next()` twice runs the
rest of the stack twice, which means two responses, two database writes, and a
`ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` thrown from a stack frame that has nothing to do with
the cause. Failing loudly at the second call is how you get a stack trace that
points at the actual bug.

**`Promise.resolve(fn(...))` lets middleware be synchronous.** A middleware
that returns `undefined` still composes. Without the wrap, `await` on
`undefined` works but a thrown synchronous error escapes the promise chain and
becomes an uncaught exception rather than a rejection.

**A middleware that forgets `await` is invisible.** `next()` without `await`
returns a floating promise; your code continues, sets a header, the response
ends, and *then* the handler below runs and writes to a finished response.
There is no compiler check for this in plain JS; in TypeScript,
`@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` catches it, which is a good reason
for that rule to be on.

**Params must be decoded once, at match time.** `/files/:name` matching
`/files/my%20report.pdf` should give `"my report.pdf"`. Decode per segment, not
on the whole path, or an encoded `/` (`%2F`) turns into a segment separator and
a parameter becomes two — the classic path-traversal-through-decoding bug.
`decodeURIComponent` also throws on malformed input like `%zz`, so it belongs
in a `try` that yields a 400 rather than a 500.

**Precedence is a score, and the score is per-segment.** A pattern's segments
each contribute: static highest, parameter middle, wildcard lowest. Compare
segment by segment, left to right, and break ties with pattern length. That
gives you `/users/me` over `/users/:id` over `/users/*` without any dependence
on registration order, and it is the same rule a radix-tree router encodes
structurally.

**405 requires you to keep the path index and the method index separate.**
Match paths first, collect every route whose pattern matched, and only then
look at methods. If no route matched at all it is a 404; if some matched but
none by method it is a 405 whose `Allow` is the sorted set of their methods —
plus `HEAD` whenever `GET` is in the set.

**Mounting must restore what it rewrote.** The two-line discipline is: save the
old path, set the new one, `await next()` in a `try`, restore in `finally`.
The `finally` is what makes it correct on the error path, and the error path is
where an unrestored path does the most damage — your error handler logs the
wrong URL for exactly the requests you most want to debug.

**Ordering is a contract, and `use` before `get` is not a style choice.** A
middleware registered after a route that responds never runs. This is obvious
until the stack is thirty entries long across six files, at which point the
only defence is a single place that declares the order and a comment saying
why. Every framework's "my auth middleware isn't running" issue is this.

**Short-circuiting is the normal case, not an escape hatch.** An auth
middleware that answers 401 and a cache middleware that answers 304 both work
by *not* calling `next`. Nothing below runs; everything above still gets its
after-phase, because those frames are suspended at their `await` and resume as
the promise chain unwinds. That is worth saying explicitly because the instinct
is to look for a `stop()` or a `return false` convention, and there is none —
returning is the mechanism.

**The response object exists so that framing rules live in one place.** Once
handlers call `ctx.send(status, value)` instead of touching `res`, every rule
from the previous sector — byte-accurate `content-length`, no body on 204, a
`HEAD` that carries the `GET` headers — is enforced in a single function. Give
handlers the raw `res` and those rules become forty separate opportunities to
get it wrong. This is the strongest argument for a framework's abstraction
layer, and it is not about typing less.

**Per-route middleware is the same mechanism at a narrower scope.**
`app.get(path, requireAuth, limitRate, handler)` is a second composed stack
that runs as the tail of the first one. Nothing new is needed to support it,
which is a good test of whether your `compose` is actually general.

## What each exercise is really testing

`ex1` is composition and the double-`next` guard. `ex2` is matching in
isolation, including decoding. `ex3` is method dispatch, 405 and `Allow`.
`ex4` is precedence as a computed score. `ex5` is errors, which in an onion are
just exceptions crossing frames. `ex6` is mounting and restoration. `ex7` is
short-circuiting — the case where a middleware answers and nothing below runs.
`ex8` is the after-phase: setting a header once the downstream work is done,
which is where `headersSent` from the previous sector comes back.

Read them as one machine being assembled rather than eight puzzles: by ex8 you
have every part a framework needs, and the challenge only has to wire them in
the right order.

The challenge builds the framework; the review compiles patterns to regexes,
which is what a router does at registration time so that matching at request
time is cheap.
