exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One recursive function with four parameters — schema, value, path, and the
issue array it pushes into — is the whole design. Returning issues instead of
throwing is what makes "report everything" free: the caller of `walk` never has
to decide whether to continue, because `walk` always does.

## Hint 2

Build the path on the way down, never on the way back up:

```ts
const child = path === "" ? key : `${path}.${key}`;
value.forEach((item, i) => walk(schema.of, item, `${path}[${i}]`, out));
```

The root being `""` is what makes `path === "" ? key : ...` necessary, and it
is worth it: an issue at the root of the document then has an empty path rather
than a leading dot, and every client can treat "empty path" as "the whole
body".

## Hint 3

The "do not descend after a type error" rule is the difference between a
usable validator and a wall of noise. If a field declared as an array arrives
as the string `"abc"`, reporting `invalid_type` once is helpful; reporting
`invalid_type` for `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]` because you iterated the string's
characters is not. Every composite branch is therefore shaped:

```ts
if (!Array.isArray(value)) { push(...); return; }   // note the return
```

The same guard on the object branch also protects you from `null`, which
`typeof` still calls `"object"` — the oldest wart in the language.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing three payloads on paper: one valid, one with a missing
required field two levels down, and one where an array item has the wrong type.
Write the exact issue list you want for each. Those become your first tests and
they will settle every ambiguity in the prompt faster than reading it again.

## Hint 2

`Object.hasOwn(value, key)` versus `key in value` is not pedantry. `in` walks
the prototype chain, so `("constructor" in {})` is `true`, and a required-field
check written with `in` accepts a payload that supplies nothing for a field
named `constructor` or `toString`. `Object.hasOwn` (Node 16.9+) is the modern
spelling of `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key)` and should be
your default everywhere, not just here.

## Hint 3

Think about what the caller does with `{ ok: true, value }`. The `value` should
be the input, unchanged — this exercise validates, it does not transform; that
is ex7's job. Keeping the two separate matters because a validator that
silently rewrites its input makes "what exactly did the client send?"
unanswerable during an incident, and because a pure check is trivially
testable.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the two primitive coercions first and make them total — a string in, a
value or `null` out — and the rest of the function becomes bookkeeping:

```ts
const asInt = (raw: string): number | null =>
  /^-?\d+$/.test(raw.trim()) ? Number(raw.trim()) : null;
```

Testing the *string* and then converting is the whole discipline. Converting
first and testing the result lets `Number("")` (which is `0`) through, and a
`limit` of 0 returns an empty page to a user who asked for a full one.

## Hint 2

Absent, ambiguous and invalid are three different outcomes and they need three
branches in this order:

```ts
const values = (query[name] ?? []).filter((v) => v.trim() !== "");
if (values.length === 0) { /* default, or required */ }
if (field.kind !== "list" && values.length > 1) { /* ambiguous */ }
```

Filtering the empties first is what makes `?page=` behave like `?` rather than
like `?page=0`.

## Hint 3

Refusing to split on commas is a real decision and worth defending. There is no
standard for repeated query parameters — `?tag=a&tag=b`, `?tag=a,b` and
`?tag[]=a&tag[]=b` all exist in the wild — so a server that supports two of
them has an ambiguity for values that contain a comma. Pick repetition,
document it, and a tag literally named `"a,b"` still round-trips. OpenAPI calls
this `style: form, explode: true`, and it is the default for a reason.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every rule in this prompt exists because a real API got it wrong. Last-wins on
`?page=1&page=99` hides parameter smuggling through a proxy. Loose integers let
`?limit=1e9` through. Empty-string-as-zero is the most common cause of "the
list is empty and I don't know why". Read the list as a set of incident reports
and the strictness stops feeling pedantic.

## Hint 2

Consider what happens with a scalar declared as `int` and given
`?page=1&page=2` in the *ambiguous* branch: you could pick the first, pick the
last, or refuse. Express picks... an array, silently, which then fails a
`Number()` in surprising ways. Refusing is the only option that cannot produce
a wrong answer, and it costs the client one clear error message once.

## Hint 3

Keep the output shape uniform: a `Record<string, unknown>` that contains
exactly the keys in `spec` — defaults filled in, unknown query keys dropped.
That way the caller can hand it to a schema check or straight to a query
builder without wondering whether a key exists. A coercion layer that sometimes
omits keys pushes `?? default` into every call site, which is where the
defaults then drift apart.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — the gate before the parser

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Export `parseMediaType(value)` and
`checkRequestBody(headers, options)`.

`parseMediaType("Application/JSON; charset=UTF-8; boundary=x")` returns
`{ type: "application/json", parameters: { charset: "utf-8", boundary: "x" } }`
— type and parameter *names* lowercased, `charset` lowercased as a value too
(it is case-insensitive by definition), other parameter values left alone,
quoted values unquoted. An unparseable value returns `null`.

`checkRequestBody(headers, { consumes, allowSuffix })` decides whether you are
willing to read the body at all, returning
`{ ok: true; type: string | null }` or `{ ok: false; status: number; code: string }`:

- no body at all — neither `content-length` nor `transfer-encoding` — is
  `{ ok: true, type: null }`, even with no `content-type`;
- `content-length: 0` counts as no body;
- a body with no `content-type` is `415` / `missing_content_type` (never sniff
  the bytes);
- an unparseable `content-type` is `400` / `malformed_content_type`;
- a type not in `consumes` is `415` / `unsupported_media_type` — unless
  `allowSuffix` is true and the type ends in `+json` while `consumes` includes
  `application/json`, which accepts `application/vnd.api+json`;
- a `charset` parameter other than `utf-8` is `415` / `unsupported_charset`;
  an absent `charset` is fine, because JSON is UTF-8 by definition.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why sniffing is forbidden rather than merely discouraged. A server that
parses a body as JSON regardless of `content-type` accepts
`content-type: text/plain`, which is one of the three types an HTML form can
send without triggering a CORS preflight. That turns a JSON API endpoint into
something a hostile page can POST to with the user's cookies attached — the
classic CSRF hole. Requiring `application/json` makes the browser preflight,
and the preflight is what your CORS policy gets to refuse.

## Hint 2

"No body" needs care because there are three spellings: no `content-length`
and no `transfer-encoding` at all; `content-length: 0`; and
`transfer-encoding: chunked` with an immediate terminating chunk, which you
cannot know from headers. Handle the first two structurally and treat the
third as "there is a body" — you will read zero bytes and find out, which is
correct and cheap.

## Hint 3

`charset` deserves its rule. JSON is defined as UTF-8, so the parameter is
redundant when present and correct — but when it says `iso-8859-1`, the client
is telling you it encoded the bytes differently, and decoding them as UTF-8
will produce mojibake or a replacement character rather than an error. Refusing
is more honest than silently corrupting a customer's name.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build the document as an object literal in the order you want, adding optional
fields conditionally, and let `JSON.stringify` preserve insertion order for
string keys. Then the `content-length` is `Buffer.byteLength` of the result —
one more place where a string's `.length` would be wrong the first time a
`detail` contains a non-ASCII character.

## Hint 2

The validation rules are all `TypeError` because they are *your* mistakes, not
a client's: a bad `status` or a relative `type` means the developer wrote the
call wrong, and it should fail in the test suite rather than produce a
malformed error response in production. The taxonomy from `04_events_errors`
again — programmer errors crash, operational errors get handled.

## Hint 3

Checking that a `type` is absolute is one line and worth understanding:

```ts
const absolute = init.type === "about:blank" || URL.canParse(init.type);
```

`URL.canParse` (Node 18.17+) is the non-throwing form of `new URL(...)`, so you
do not need a `try`. `about:blank` is the RFC's own default and means "no
further identification", which is the honest value for an error you have not
bothered to categorise yet.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what a client does with each field. `type` is the only one they should
branch on, so it is the only one that must be stable forever. `title` is for a
human reading a log. `detail` is about this occurrence and may contain numbers.
`instance` identifies the specific request, which is what a support ticket
quotes. `errors` is what a form uses. Writing that mapping down is how you stop
yourself from putting a stack trace in `detail`.

## Hint 2

The key-order rule looks fussy and pays for itself in review. Two error bodies
that differ only in key order produce a diff that hides the one field that
actually changed, and snapshot tests become noisy enough that people stop
reading them. Insertion order for string keys has been guaranteed by the
language since ES2015 — integer-like keys are the exception, and error
documents do not have those.

## Hint 3

Consider what `about:blank` buys you. RFC 9457 says a `type` of `about:blank`
means the problem has no additional semantics beyond the HTTP status, and that
the `title` should then be the status phrase. That gives you a legitimate,
standard-shaped response for the boring 500 without inventing a URI you will
never write documentation for — and it makes the ones you *do* name
meaningful by contrast.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — from a thrown thing to a response

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Export `createErrorMapper(registry, options)` returning
`toProblem(error, instance)`.

```ts
interface Entry { status: number; type: string; title: string }
type Registry = Record<string, Entry>;   // keyed by error.code
```

`toProblem` turns anything that was thrown into the `{ status, headers, body }`
shape from ex4 (copy `problem` in):

- an error whose `code` is a string present in `registry` uses that entry's
  `status`, `type` and `title`, and its own `message` as `detail`;
- an error carrying an `issues` array puts it in `errors`;
- anything else — an unknown code, a thrown string, `undefined`, an `Error`
  with no code — becomes `500`, `about:blank`, title `"Internal Server Error"`,
  and `detail` exactly `"An unexpected error occurred."` **The original message
  must not appear anywhere in the body.**
- every document carries the extension `requestId`, taken from
  `options.requestId()`;
- `options.report(error)` is called for 5xx only, and exactly once per call;
- a registry entry with a 5xx status is honoured for the status but still gets
  the flattened detail — a registered internal failure is still an internal
  failure as far as the client is concerned.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The registry is the seam between your domain vocabulary and HTTP. Domain code
throws `Object.assign(new Error("no such order"), { code: "order_not_found" })`
and never mentions 404; the mapper owns the translation. That separation is why
you can change a status across the whole API by editing one table, and why
domain code is testable without HTTP.

## Hint 2

Extract the code defensively, because you are handed `unknown`:

```ts
const code = (error as { code?: unknown } | null)?.code;
const entry = typeof code === "string" ? registry[code] : undefined;
```

`(x as ...)?.code` on a string or `null` yields `undefined` rather than
throwing. Note also that a registry lookup with an attacker-influenced key
should use `Object.hasOwn(registry, code)` or a `Map`, or `code` of
`"constructor"` finds something surprising.

## Hint 3

The 5xx rule has two halves and both matter. The client gets a fixed sentence,
because a 5xx message is your stack talking and it names hosts, tables and file
paths. Your logs get the real error through `report`, with the `requestId` so
the two can be joined. Getting that pairing right is what makes an error body
that says nothing still be debuggable in thirty seconds.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think of `toProblem` as the only place in the service that decides what a
stranger learns about a failure. Every other layer either throws with a code or
passes the error along. Concentrating the decision means the review question
"could this leak?" has exactly one file to look at.

## Hint 2

Why `report` fires only for 5xx: 4xx are the client's mistakes and they arrive
in volume, from scanners, from misconfigured integrations, from someone's
retry loop. Sending them to an error tracker turns the tracker into a firehose
and trains your team to ignore it. Count 4xx as a metric with a rate; report
5xx as events with stacks.

## Hint 3

The subtle case is a *registered* 5xx — say `upstream_unavailable` mapped to
503. The status and `type` come from the registry (the client can branch on
"the upstream is down" and retry), but `detail` must still be flattened,
because the message underneath is `connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.14:5432` and
that is your network topology. Keeping those two decisions separate — status
from the registry, detail from the status class — is the whole point of the
exercise.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — the rules a schema cannot express

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Export `checkOrder(order)` and `statusFor(issues)`.

`checkOrder` receives an order that has **already passed** a shape check, so
every field has the right type. It returns the semantic issues — the rules that
are about meaning rather than form:

```ts
interface Order {
  currency: string; items: Array<{ sku: string; quantity: number; unitPrice: number }>;
  discount: number; startsAt: string; endsAt: string;    // ISO 8601
}
```

- `items` must have at least one entry → `empty_order` at path `items`;
- duplicate `sku` values → `duplicate_sku` at the path of the **second**
  occurrence, e.g. `items[2].sku`;
- `currency` must be one of `GBP`, `EUR`, `USD` → `unsupported_currency`;
- `discount` must not exceed the subtotal (sum of `quantity * unitPrice`) →
  `discount_exceeds_total` at `discount`;
- `startsAt` and `endsAt` must both parse as dates → `invalid_date`, and
  `endsAt` must be strictly after `startsAt` → `end_before_start` at `endsAt`;
- money is compared in **integer minor units** — `unitPrice` is already in
  pence, so no floating-point comparison anywhere.

`statusFor(issues)` returns `400` if any issue's code is in the syntax set
(`invalid_type`, `required`, `invalid_format`, `invalid_json`), `422` if there
are issues and none are syntactic, and `200` for an empty list.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors ex6
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Money is the part of this exercise that will follow you into every job.
`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` in every IEEE-754 language, so a subtotal built from
floating-point pounds drifts, and a comparison against a discount is then
occasionally wrong in a way that shows up as a penny in a reconciliation report
three weeks later. Integer minor units — pence, cents — plus a single
formatting step at the edge is the standard answer, and "why is `unitPrice` an
integer?" is a good interview question to be able to answer.

## Hint 2

`statusFor` is where you make the 400-versus-422 argument concrete. The
defensible line: 400 means the request could not be understood as the kind of
thing you accept; 422 means it was understood and is unacceptable. Note the
consequence for clients — a 400 says "your serialiser or your code is wrong",
a 422 says "your user's input is wrong" — and that is exactly the difference
between a developer's bug and a form field turning red.

## Hint 3

Order the checks so that later ones do not depend on facts earlier ones just
disproved. Computing a subtotal over an empty item list gives 0, which then
makes any non-zero discount "exceed the total" — two issues for one problem,
and the second is noise. Either return early on `empty_order` or skip the
discount check when there are no items. Deciding this consciously is what keeps
an issue list short enough for a human to act on.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — only the keys you asked for

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Export
`sanitize(fields, input, options)`.

```ts
interface FieldRule { trim?: boolean; lower?: boolean; emptyAsAbsent?: boolean }

function sanitize(
  fields: Record<string, FieldRule>,
  input: Record<string, unknown>,
  options: { unknown: "strip" | "reject" },
): { value: Record<string, unknown>; issues: Issue[] };
```

- The result contains **only** keys declared in `fields`. Nothing is copied
  because it happened to be there.
- `trim` trims a string value; `lower` lowercases it; both ignore non-string
  values rather than coercing them.
- `emptyAsAbsent` drops a key whose value is `""` after trimming.
- `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` are never copied even if declared,
  and their presence in `input` is an issue with code `forbidden_key` — in
  both modes.
- `unknown: "reject"` adds an `unknown_key` issue per undeclared key, sorted by
  key name so the output is stable; `unknown: "strip"` adds nothing.
- `input` must not be mutated.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The rule that makes this safe is "build the output, do not filter the input".
Iterate `fields` and pull values across; never iterate `input` and delete what
you dislike. A denylist is a list of the attacks you have thought of; an
allowlist is a list of what your code actually uses.

## Hint 2

The mass-assignment story is the reason this exists. A handler that does
`await db.users.update(id, req.body)` lets a client set any column — `role`,
`accountId`, `emailVerified`. Rails had this as a famous CVE in 2012 (someone
committed to the Rails repo through it), and every ORM since has an
allowlisting mechanism. `sanitize` is that mechanism, written out.

## Hint 3

The forbidden keys are about prototype pollution. `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":
{"admin": true}}')` gives you an object with an *own* `__proto__` property, and
a copy loop that assigns it onto a fresh object can end up writing to
`Object.prototype`, at which point every object in the process has `admin`.
Two defences, and using both is normal: skip those three keys explicitly, and
prefer `Object.hasOwn` over `in` when checking presence.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice which transformations are listed and which are not. `trim` and `lower`
are safe because they are idempotent and lossless in the ways that matter for
identifiers. Nothing here truncates, escapes HTML, or "cleans" a value. That
is deliberate: escaping belongs at the output boundary, where you know whether
the destination is HTML, SQL or a shell — sanitising at input produces data
that is wrong for every destination and right for none.

## Hint 2

Think about `emptyAsAbsent` as an argument the API design is having with
itself. An HTML form submits every field, so a blank optional input arrives as
`""`. Is that "clear this value" or "I did not touch it"? Both readings are
common; the rule makes the choice explicit per field, which is the only honest
way to handle it. `null` for "clear" and absent for "unchanged" is the other
convention, and JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) formalises it.

## Hint 3

"Must not mutate `input`" is worth a moment. Shared mutable request data is
how a logging middleware ends up printing the sanitised body instead of the
received one, which makes an incident unreconstructable. Build a new object,
return it, and let the caller decide what to keep. The same reasoning as the
ex1 rule that validation does not transform.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — a validator an attacker cannot make expensive

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Export `collectIssues(schema, value, limits)` using the
ex1 `Schema` (copy it in).

```ts
interface Limits { maxIssues: number; maxDepth: number; maxItems: number }
function collectIssues(schema: Schema, value: unknown, limits: Limits):
  { issues: Issue[]; truncated: boolean };
```

Three caps, each closing a way to spend your CPU or your log budget:

- **`maxIssues`** — stop walking as soon as the list reaches the cap, append
  one final issue `{ path: "", code: "truncated", message: ... }`, and report
  `truncated: true`. The final issue is not itself counted against the cap and
  is added exactly once.
- **`maxDepth`** — the root is depth 0; a value at depth greater than
  `maxDepth` is reported as `too_deep` at its path and not descended into.
- **`maxItems`** — an array longer than `maxItems` gets one `too_many_items`
  issue at its own path and only its first `maxItems` entries are validated.

Everything else behaves exactly as ex1.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

All three caps are the same idea: a validator's cost is a function of input the
client controls, so every dimension of that input needs a bound. Body size was
bounded two sectors ago; this is the same argument applied to nesting depth,
array length, and how much you are willing to say about a bad document.

## Hint 2

The stop condition wants to be checked in one place — at the top of the
recursive step — rather than sprinkled after every `push`:

```ts
const walk = (schema, value, path, depth) => {
  if (issues.length >= limits.maxIssues) return;     // one guard
  if (depth > limits.maxDepth) { push(path, "too_deep", ...); return; }
  ...
};
```

Adding the `truncated` marker once, after the walk returns, keeps that logic
out of the recursion entirely.

## Hint 3

`maxDepth` protects against a payload like `{"a":{"a":{"a":...}}}` nested ten
thousand deep. Note that `JSON.parse` itself will happily build that (it is
iterative in V8 and does not overflow), so the depth problem lands squarely on
*your* recursion — which does use the stack, and will throw
`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` rather than returning a 400.
A `RangeError` escaping into a 500 is a bad way to learn this.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the attacker gets from each unbounded dimension. Deep nesting: a stack
overflow, which is an uncatchable-in-practice crash of the whole process, so
every concurrent request dies with it. Huge arrays: quadratic behaviour if any
of your checks is `O(n)` per item. Unbounded issues: a 40 MB response and a log
line that fills a disk. The last one is the least dramatic and the most common.

## Hint 2

There is a design tension in `maxIssues` worth naming. Truncating at, say, 50
issues means a client with 200 bad fields fixes 50, resubmits, and gets 50
more. That is annoying but bounded; the alternative is a response that is
itself a denial of service. Say so in the truncation message — "the first 50
of many problems" — so the client's developer knows to expect another round
rather than concluding your validator is flaky.

## Hint 3

An honest note on `maxItems`: validating only the first N items means you will
report an order with 10,000 lines as having a problem in line 3 while saying
nothing about line 9,000. That is fine, because the request is already being
rejected for `too_many_items` — the array cap is a *business* rule as much as a
defence, and a real API states its maximum in its documentation rather than
discovering it under load.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — one endpoint, every gate

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createOrdersHandler({ requestId, report })`
returns a `node:http` handler for `POST /orders` in which every layer of this
sector runs in the right order, and each failure produces the right status and
a `application/problem+json` body.

The pipeline, in order — and the order is graded, because each step assumes the
previous one succeeded:

1. **Method and path.** Anything else is `404` (`about:blank`).
2. **Media type.** No `content-type` on a body → `415`
   `missing_content_type`; not `application/json` (or `+json`) → `415`
   `unsupported_media_type`; a non-UTF-8 `charset` → `415`.
3. **Size.** Bodies over 16384 bytes → `413` `payload_too_large`, refused from
   `content-length` when it is declared and from a running total when it is
   not.
4. **Syntax.** Unparseable JSON → `400` `invalid_json`. A body that is not a
   JSON object (an array, a number, `null`) → `400` `invalid_type`.
5. **Shape.** The order schema: `currency` string of length 3, `items` a
   non-empty array of `{ sku: string, quantity: integer ≥ 1, unitPrice:
   integer ≥ 0 }`, `discount` an integer ≥ 0, `startsAt` and `endsAt` strings.
   Failures → `422` with an `errors` array of `{path, code, message}`.
6. **Unknown keys.** Rejected at the top level → `422` with `unknown_key`
   issues.
7. **Semantics.** The ex6 rules → `422`.
8. **Success.** `201`, `location: /orders/ord-N` counting from 1, and a JSON
   body `{ id, subtotal, total }` with `total = subtotal - discount`, both in
   minor units.

Every problem document carries `instance` (the request path) and a
`requestId` extension. `report` is called for 5xx only. An unexpected throw is
`500` with `detail` exactly `"An unexpected error occurred."`

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write it as a sequence of small functions that each return "ok" or a problem,
and one `handler` that runs them in order and returns at the first failure. The
temptation is a single function with nested `if`s; the cost is that you cannot
test step 5 without constructing a request that gets past steps 1 to 4.

## Hint 2

The ordering is not arbitrary, and being able to say why is the point. Cheap
before expensive: headers before bytes, bytes before parsing, parsing before
walking a schema, schema before semantics. Also *safe* before *unsafe*: you
must know the media type before you agree to buffer, and you must know the
shape before code that assumes `order.items.length` runs.

## Hint 3

The success path has two small traps. `total` can be computed from values you
have already validated, so no re-checking — but it must be an integer, which it
is only because `unitPrice` and `discount` are. And `location` is a relative
reference (`/orders/ord-1`), which RFC 9110 has allowed since 2014; an absolute
URL would require you to trust the `Host` header, which the review in the first
sector of this volume showed is not free.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Keep one function that builds problem documents and call it from every failure
branch. Nine failure branches each writing their own `res.writeHead` is nine
opportunities to forget the `content-type`, the `content-length`, or the
`requestId` — and the one you forget will be the branch that only fires in
production.

## Hint 2

Two behaviours worth checking by hand before running the gate:

- a body of exactly 16384 bytes is accepted and 16385 is refused (the limit is
  inclusive, and off-by-one here is the kind of bug that only appears for one
  customer);
- an `items` array that is present but empty produces the `empty_order`
  semantic issue, not a schema `too_small` — decide which layer owns the rule
  and do not let both report it, or the client sees the same problem twice with
  two different codes.

## Hint 3

For the unexpected-throw path, remember that your handler is a callback that
nobody awaits. The whole body of the async work needs a `.catch` that maps to a
500 problem document, and that `catch` must itself be careful: if the headers
are already sent there is nothing to write, and the only remaining option is to
destroy the response. Writing a second header block throws
`ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` from inside your error handler, which is how a service
turns one bad request into a crash.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the sentence a person reads

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Issues are for machines; forms are for people.
Export `explainIssue(issue)` and `fieldErrors(issues)`.

`explainIssue({ path, code, message })` returns one sentence with a
human-readable label built from the path:

- the last segment names the field, split on camelCase and lowercased except
  for the first word: `shipTo.postCode` → `"Post code"`, `unitPrice` →
  `"Unit price"`;
- an index in the path is spoken as a one-based position: `items[0].quantity`
  → `"Quantity (item 1)"`, `items[2]` → `"Item 3"`;
- an empty path is `"This request"`;
- the sentence is `` `${label} ${message}` `` with a full stop appended when
  the message does not already end in one — so
  `{ path: "items[0].quantity", code: "too_small", message: "must be at least 1" }`
  gives `"Quantity (item 1) must be at least 1."`

`fieldErrors(issues)` groups messages by path into
`Record<string, string[]>` for a form renderer: insertion order preserved,
identical messages under one path de-duplicated, and no prototype-polluting
key ever used as a property name.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb03_validation_errors review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take the path apart before you try to phrase anything. `items[0].quantity`
splits into the field name (`quantity`) and the trailing index of its container
(`0`). The two cases — a named field inside an indexed container, and an
indexed element itself — are the only two shapes, so a small regex or a split
on `.` and a check for a trailing `[n]` covers it.

## Hint 2

camelCase to words is one replace and one case fix:

```ts
const words = name.replace(/([a-z0-9])([A-Z])/g, "$1 $2").toLowerCase();
const label = words.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + words.slice(1);
```

The lookahead-free form handles `postCode` and `unitPrice`. It does not handle
`SKU` or `orderID` gracefully, and that is worth noticing rather than papering
over: real form libraries take an explicit label map, because English is not
derivable from an identifier.

## Hint 3

For `fieldErrors`, build the record with `Object.create(null)` or guard the
three forbidden names before using a path as a key. It is the same lesson as
ex7 arriving from a different direction: any time a string you did not choose
becomes a property name, prototype pollution is one payload away.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about who calls each function. `explainIssue` is for a server-rendered
page or a plain-text client. `fieldErrors` is for a form: a React component
looks up `errors["shipTo.postCode"]` and renders the strings under that input.
Neither replaces the raw issue list, which is what a machine consumes. Three
audiences, three shapes, one source — and the source is the one you must not
break.

## Hint 2

The one-based index rule is a small usability decision with real consequences.
Zero-based is correct for a program and wrong for a person: "item 0" makes a
user count wrong on the screen in front of them. Every place your code faces a
human — line numbers, page numbers, list positions — has this conversion, and
doing it in one place beats doing it in six templates.

## Hint 3

De-duplication in `fieldErrors` is not a formatting nicety. Two layers can
legitimately produce the same message for the same field — a schema check and a
semantic check both saying "must be at least 1" — and a form that shows it
twice looks broken. Deduplicating on the message string is the cheap fix;
deduplicating on `code` is the better one if you have it, because two different
codes with identical wording are a message-writing problem you want to see.

lessons.title: V3·NB4 — Authentication, sessions and tokens
lessons.summary: Authentication is a small amount of cryptography surrounded by a large amount of protocol detail, and the protocol detail is where services get broken. This sector builds it from node:crypto: constant-time comparison, scrypt password hashing, HMAC-signed cookies with key rotation, a JWT verifier that refuses alg confusion, session fixation and idle expiry, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, and the 401-versus-403 decision.

# V3·NB4 — Authentication, sessions and tokens

Every request in the previous sectors was anonymous. Adding identity introduces
a new category of bug, because authentication code fails *silently correct*: a
signature check with `===` instead of a constant-time compare still returns the
right answer for every test you will write, and is still broken. The mistakes
here are not caught by types, tests or code review unless the reviewer already
knows what to look for.

So this sector is deliberately mechanical. You will build the primitives out of
`node:crypto` — no `jsonwebtoken`, no `passport`, no `cookie-session` — because
the shape of the mistakes is only visible from inside.

## Three questions that are not the same

**Authentication** is "who is this?" **Session management** is "how do I keep
knowing, across requests, without asking again?" **Authorization** is "may they
do this?" Systems that blur them produce the two most common access-control
bugs in web software: an endpoint that checks you are logged in but not that
the record belongs to you, and a token that proves who you are but carries
permissions that were true ten minutes ago.

The HTTP status codes encode the distinction, and they are routinely swapped.
`401 Unauthorized` means *unauthenticated*: no credentials, or bad ones. It is
required to carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header saying what scheme you want —
almost nobody does, and it is one line. `403 Forbidden` means authenticated and
not permitted; sending credentials again will not help. If you send 401 for a
permission failure, a well-behaved client will loop trying to re-authenticate.

## Two ways to remember, and their trade

**Server-side sessions.** The client holds an opaque random id in a cookie; the
server holds the state. Revocation is a delete. The cost is a lookup per
request and shared storage between instances.

**Tokens (JWT and friends).** The client holds a signed document containing the
claims; the server verifies the signature and reads them. No lookup, no shared
storage. The cost is that you cannot take it back — a stolen token is valid
until it expires, which is why access tokens are minutes long and are paired
with refresh tokens you *can* revoke, which means you have a database again.

The honest summary: JWTs solve a scaling problem most services do not have, and
introduce a revocation problem every service does have. For a first-party web
app, a session cookie is usually the better default. For service-to-service
calls and short-lived access tokens in an OAuth flow, a JWT is the right tool.
Knowing why is more valuable than knowing either API.

## The cryptography, briefly

Four primitives cover everything here, and all four are in `node:crypto`.

`timingSafeEqual` compares two buffers in time independent of where they
differ. `a === b` on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, and
that difference is measurable across a network with enough samples. It throws
if the lengths differ, which is why you hash both sides to a fixed length
first — the length itself leaks nothing useful, but the throw is a bug you will
otherwise hit in production on a truncated token.

`scrypt` (or Argon2 via a native module) turns a password into a hash slowly
and with a memory cost, so that an attacker with your database cannot test
billions of guesses per second. A salt per password stops one precomputed table
from covering everyone. Never `sha256` a password; SHA-256 is designed to be
fast, which is exactly wrong here.

`createHmac` produces a keyed hash: a tag that only someone with the key can
produce, and anyone with the key can verify. It is what signs a session cookie
and what signs an HS256 JWT.

`randomBytes` / `randomUUID` produce unpredictable values. `Math.random()` is
not a CSPRNG and has been the root cause of a long list of session-prediction
vulnerabilities.

## Where the credential lives in a browser

There is a recurring argument about whether to keep a token in `localStorage`
or a cookie, and it has an answer. `localStorage` is readable by any script
running on the page, so any cross-site scripting bug — including one in a
dependency, an analytics snippet or an ad — becomes complete account takeover,
with the token exfiltrated and usable from anywhere until it expires. An
`HttpOnly` cookie is not reachable from JavaScript at all, so the same XSS can
act *as* the user while the page is open but cannot walk away with the
credential.

The counter-argument is that cookies are sent automatically and therefore
enable CSRF. That was decisive before `SameSite`; it is much weaker now that
`Lax` is the browser default, and it is fully answered by a double-submit token
— a random value in a readable cookie that your JavaScript copies into a
header, which a cross-site attacker can cause to be *sent* but cannot *read*.
You will build exactly that in the challenge.

## Cost, and the shape of the mistakes

Two more habits that separate working code from correct code here.

Everything that gates access is compared in constant time. Not because a
timing attack is easy — over the public internet it is genuinely hard — but
because the rule is cheap to apply universally and impossible to apply
selectively without eventually misjudging which value was secret.

And every check fails closed. An unparseable stored hash denies rather than
throws; an action with no policy is refused rather than allowed; an unknown
signing key rejects rather than falling back to a default. Authentication code
meets malformed input as its normal case, because that input is chosen by
someone who wants it to be malformed.

## What the exercises cover

Constant-time comparison and `Authorization` parsing; password hashing with
scrypt; signed cookies with a key ring so keys can rotate without logging
everyone out; cookie attributes, where `HttpOnly`, `SameSite` and the
`__Host-` prefix each close a specific attack; an HS256 JWT verifier that
refuses `alg: none` and algorithm confusion; sessions with fixation defence and
two kinds of expiry; refresh rotation with reuse detection; and the
authorization check itself, including resource ownership.

Then a challenge that wires a login, a session and a CSRF defence together, and
a review on parsing credentials.

# Reading - node/v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens

Notes on the primitives, the protocol details around them, and the failure
modes that do not show up in tests.

## Notes

**`timingSafeEqual` needs equal lengths, so hash first.** The standard shape is
`timingSafeEqual(sha256(a), sha256(b))`: both sides are 32 bytes, the compare
cannot throw, and the hashing is fast enough not to matter. Comparing raw
strings with `===` leaks a byte at a time; comparing buffers of different
lengths throws and you learn about it from a 500.

**Password hashing is a cost parameter, not an algorithm choice.** scrypt's
`N`, `r`, `p` (Node's defaults: 16384, 8, 1) set CPU and memory work. Argon2id
is the current recommendation where a native module is acceptable; scrypt is
the strongest thing in the standard library and is fine. Store the parameters
*with* the hash — `scrypt$16384$8$1$salt$hash` — or you can never raise the
cost without invalidating every password.

**Verification must be constant time and must not reveal existence.** Two
requirements that interact: use `timingSafeEqual` on the derived keys, and when
the user does not exist, hash *something* anyway before answering, so "no such
user" and "wrong password" take the same time and return the same message.
Otherwise your login form is a user enumeration oracle.

**A signed cookie is `value.signature`, and rotation needs a key ring.**
Signing with the newest key and verifying against all of them lets you retire a
key by removing it from the list a week later, rather than logging everyone out
at once. Adding a key id to the token makes verification a lookup instead of a
loop, which is what JWTs do with `kid`.

**Cookie attributes are the actual security.** `HttpOnly` keeps JavaScript, and
therefore an XSS payload, away from the value. `Secure` keeps it off plaintext
HTTP. `SameSite=Lax` stops it being sent on cross-site POSTs, which is most of
CSRF; `Strict` also stops it on top-level navigation, which logs users out when
they follow a link from an email. The `__Host-` prefix is enforced by browsers:
a cookie so named must be `Secure`, have `Path=/`, and have **no** `Domain`,
which prevents a subdomain from setting a cookie your parent domain will trust.

**JWT verification is where the famous bugs live.** `alg: none` was a real
accepted value in early libraries. Algorithm confusion — a token signed with
the HMAC algorithm using your *public* RSA key as the secret — broke several
implementations. The defence is one rule: the verifier decides the algorithm,
never the token. Read `alg` only to reject it if it is not what you expected.

**`exp`, `nbf` and `iat` are seconds, not milliseconds.** `Date.now() / 1000`,
floored. A verifier should allow a small clock skew (60 seconds is
conventional) in both directions, and must treat a missing `exp` as a token
that never expires — which is a reason to require it.

**Session fixation is fixed by rotating the id at login.** If an attacker can
set a victim's session id before login (through a URL parameter, a subdomain
cookie, or an XSS) and you keep that id afterwards, they now share the
authenticated session. Issuing a *new* id at every privilege change closes it,
and it costs one line.

**Two expiries, not one.** Absolute ("this session dies 12 hours after login,
whatever happens") bounds the damage of a stolen cookie. Idle ("30 minutes
without a request") logs out the abandoned laptop. Real systems have both, and
the interaction — sliding the idle window on each request without moving the
absolute deadline — is where implementations go wrong.

**Refresh tokens rotate, and reuse means theft.** Every refresh issues a new
token and invalidates the old. If an old one is presented again, either the
network dropped a response or a thief has a copy; you cannot tell, so you
revoke the whole family. That is the OAuth 2 Security BCP's recommendation and
it is implementable in about thirty lines.

**Store what you must keep, hash what you only need to compare.** A password
gets a slow, salted KDF because it is low-entropy and an attacker with your
database can guess it. A refresh token gets a plain SHA-256 because it is
128 bits of randomness with no dictionary to attack — a slow KDF there costs
you a hundred times the CPU for nothing. Knowing why the two differ is more
useful than either rule on its own.

**Authorization checks belong in a policy, not in each handler.** The most
common access-control bug in web software is an endpoint that verifies the
caller is logged in and then loads a record without checking who owns it. It
is invisible to scanners and to code review, because the missing check is
missing. A declared policy per action — scope, roles, ownership — turns the
omission into a 403 that the first test catches.

**`no-store` on every authenticated response.** A shared cache that retains
`GET /me` hands one user's identity to another. `no-store` is the strong form;
`private, no-cache` allows a browser-local copy with revalidation, which is
sometimes right for a personalised page and never right for an identity
endpoint.

## What each exercise is really testing

`ex1` is constant-time comparison and the 401 challenge. `ex2` is scrypt and
non-enumerable verification. `ex3` is HMAC with rotation. `ex4` is cookie
attributes as policy. `ex5` is a JWT verifier that cannot be talked into
trusting the token. `ex6` is fixation and the two expiries. `ex7` is rotation
with reuse detection. `ex8` is authorization, ownership, and 401 versus 403.
The challenge assembles a login flow with CSRF; the review parses
`Authorization` for both schemes you will meet.

# V3·NB4 — Authentication, sessions and tokens (archive)

## The three questions

```
  who are you?      -> authentication  -> 401 + WWW-Authenticate
  still you?        -> session/token   -> cookie or bearer token
  may you do this?  -> authorization   -> 403
```

Keeping them separate in code — a function that identifies, a store that
remembers, a check that permits — is what stops the two classic bugs: an
endpoint that verifies login but not ownership, and a token whose permissions
are stale.

## Constant time, and why

```ts
import { createHash, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

export function safeEqual(a: string, b: string): boolean {
  // Hash first: timingSafeEqual throws on length mismatch, and the hash makes
  // both sides 32 bytes whatever arrived.
  const ha = createHash("sha256").update(a, "utf8").digest();
  const hb = createHash("sha256").update(b, "utf8").digest();
  return timingSafeEqual(ha, hb);
}
```

`a === b` on strings returns at the first differing byte. Over enough samples
that difference is measurable, and an attacker recovers a token one character
at a time. The attack is finicky over the internet and trivial over a local
network or a shared host, and the fix costs nothing.

## Passwords

```ts
import { randomBytes, scrypt, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const derive = promisify(scrypt) as (p: string, s: Buffer, k: number) => Promise<Buffer>;

export async function hashPassword(password: string): Promise<string> {
  const salt = randomBytes(16);
  const key = await derive(password.normalize("NFKC"), salt, 64);
  return `scrypt$16384$8$1$${salt.toString("base64url")}$${key.toString("base64url")}`;
}
```

Four decisions in five lines: a random per-password salt, a slow memory-hard
function, the parameters stored *in* the string so the cost can be raised
later, and Unicode normalisation so that two spellings of the same accented
password match.

Verification must not leak whether the user exists:

```ts
const stored = await users.find(email);
const record = stored ?? DUMMY_HASH;     // always do the work
const ok = await verify(record, password);
return stored !== undefined && ok;
```

Common mistakes:

- **`sha256(password)`** — fast is the opposite of what you want.
- **A global salt, or none** — one rainbow table covers every user.
- **Returning early when the user is missing** — a timing oracle that
  enumerates your customers.
- **Trimming or lowercasing the password** — it silently shrinks the keyspace,
  and users who paste a trailing space are then locked out inconsistently.

## Signed cookies with rotation

```ts
export function sign(value: string, keys: Key[]): string {
  const key = keys[0];                                    // newest signs
  const mac = createHmac("sha256", key.secret).update(`${key.id}.${value}`)
    .digest("base64url");
  return `${key.id}.${value}.${mac}`;
}
```

Verification looks the key up by id and compares in constant time. The key ring
is what makes rotation a deployment rather than an outage: add a new key at the
front, keep the old one for a week, then drop it. A single-key design forces a
choice between never rotating and logging everyone out.

## Cookie attributes as policy

| attribute | attack it addresses |
| --- | --- |
| `HttpOnly` | XSS reading the session value |
| `Secure` | plaintext interception, and downgrade |
| `SameSite=Lax` | cross-site POST (most CSRF) |
| `Path=/`, no `Domain` | a sibling subdomain setting cookies you trust |
| `__Host-` prefix | browser enforcement of the two rules above |
| `Max-Age` | an unbounded lifetime for a stolen cookie |

## JWT, verified properly

```ts
const [h, p, s] = token.split(".");
const header = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(h, "base64url").toString());
if (header.alg !== "HS256") throw badToken("unexpected_alg");   // WE decide
const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${h}.${p}`).digest();
if (!timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(s, "base64url"), expected)) throw badToken("bad_signature");
```

The single rule that prevents the famous JWT vulnerabilities: **the verifier
chooses the algorithm.** `alg: none` and RS256-to-HS256 confusion both work by
persuading the library to take the token's word for it.

## Sessions: fixation and two deadlines

```ts
start(userId, previousId) {
  if (previousId !== undefined) sessions.delete(previousId);   // fixation
  const id = newId();
  const at = now();
  sessions.set(id, { userId, createdAt: at, lastSeenAt: at });
  return id;
}

const expired = (s: Session, at: number) =>
  at >= s.lastSeenAt + idleMs || at >= s.createdAt + absoluteMs;
```

Session fixation is the attack where someone plants an id on a victim — a URL
parameter, a cookie set by a sibling subdomain, an XSS — and waits for them to
log in. If the id survives the login, the planted copy is now authenticated.
Issuing a new id at every privilege change is the entire defence and costs one
line.

The two deadlines answer different threats. Idle expiry logs out the abandoned
laptop. Absolute expiry bounds a stolen cookie that is being used constantly,
so the idle timer never fires. `touch` slides `lastSeenAt` and must not move
`createdAt`, or you have one deadline and it is the weaker one.

## Refresh rotation, and what reuse means

A refresh token is single use. Present an old one and there are two
explanations: the client never received the response carrying its replacement,
or somebody else has a copy. You cannot tell which, so you assume the worse and
revoke the whole family. The legitimate user re-authenticates; the thief is
locked out. That asymmetry is why the OAuth 2 Security BCP recommends it for
public clients, and why the false positives are acceptable.

Store the tokens hashed. Unlike passwords, a plain SHA-256 is enough — there is
no dictionary to attack a 128-bit random value with — but a database dump must
not be a set of live credentials.

## The interview answers

*"Session or JWT?"* Sessions for first-party web apps: revocation is a delete
and the lookup is cheap. JWTs for short-lived access tokens between services,
paired with a revocable refresh token. The trade is revocation versus
statelessness, not security versus convenience.

*"Where do you store a token in a browser?"* An `HttpOnly` cookie, with
`SameSite` and a CSRF defence. `localStorage` is readable by any script on the
page, which turns any XSS into full account takeover.

*"401 or 403?"* 401 means "I do not know who you are" and must carry
`WWW-Authenticate`. 403 means "I know, and no".

## Authorization, as a table rather than as code

```ts
const policies = {
  "orders:read":   { scope: "orders.read",  ownership: true },
  "orders:delete": { scope: "orders.write", roles: ["staff"], ownership: true },
  "reports:run":   { roles: ["analyst", "admin"] },
};
```

Three properties fall out of writing it down. An action with no entry is denied,
so a new endpoint is refused until someone states the rule — the omission
becomes loud instead of invisible. Scope and role are checked separately,
because they answer different questions: a scope is what the *client
application* was granted on the user's behalf, a role is what the *user* may
do, and a support agent using a read-only integration should still not be able
to write. And ownership is a flag rather than something each handler
remembers, which is the difference between a policy and a convention.

The `admin` bypass, if you have one, relaxes ownership only. A broad "admins
can do anything" branch at the top is how an admin token with a read-only
scope ends up deleting records.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `timingSafeEqual` throw on a length mismatch, and what do you do
   about it?
2. Why hash a password slowly?
3. What must be stored alongside a password hash, and why?
4. How do you avoid user enumeration on a login endpoint?
5. What does a key ring buy you over a single signing secret?
6. What does the `__Host-` prefix require, and which attack does that stop?
7. Why must the verifier, not the token, choose the JWT algorithm?
8. What are the units of `exp`, and how much skew should you allow?
9. What is session fixation and what single change prevents it?
10. Why have both an absolute and an idle session expiry?
11. What does refresh-token reuse imply, and what should happen?
12. Which status code does a permission failure get, and why not the other one?
13. Why is `localStorage` a bad place for a session token?

# Identity on the web, and how it actually breaks

## Why this code is different

Most bugs announce themselves. Authentication bugs do not: a broken signature
check accepts good tokens, a timing leak returns correct answers, a session
that never rotates behaves identically to one that does. The feedback loop that
normally teaches you — write it, run it, see it fail — is absent, which is why
this area is taught as a list of rules rather than derived from first
principles. The rules are the compressed form of other people's incidents.

## Passwords, and the arms race in the cost parameter

A password hash is a deliberately slow function. That is the whole design:
your server does the work once per login, an attacker with a stolen database
does it once per guess. The parameters encode how slow, and they have to move
with hardware — a cost that was reasonable in 2015 is a rounding error on a
2026 GPU.

bcrypt (1999) introduced the idea of a tunable cost and is still fine. scrypt
(2009) added a memory cost, because memory is the expensive part of a GPU or
ASIC attack. Argon2 (2015) won the Password Hashing Competition and Argon2id
is the current default recommendation. Node ships scrypt in the standard
library and nothing else, which makes it the pragmatic choice unless you are
willing to take a native dependency.

Storing the parameters with the hash is the operational detail that separates a
system that can improve from one that cannot. `scrypt$16384$8$1$salt$hash`
tells a future verifier exactly how to reproduce the derivation, which means
you can raise the cost for new passwords, and re-hash old ones opportunistically
at the next successful login.

## Sessions versus tokens, without the marketing

The JWT enthusiasm of the mid-2010s was mostly about horizontal scaling: if
verification needs no shared state, any instance can serve any request. That
argument is real and it is smaller than it sounds, because a session lookup
against Redis is a sub-millisecond operation that you are probably already
doing for other reasons.

What the enthusiasm skipped is revocation. A signed token is valid until it
expires, by construction — that is what "stateless" means. Logging out,
banning an account, or responding to a stolen laptop all require either a very
short lifetime (so you are back to frequent refreshes) or a denylist (so you
are back to shared state). The mature pattern that fell out of this is the
one OAuth 2 codifies: a short-lived access token that is a JWT, and a
long-lived refresh token that is an opaque random string in a database, where
revocation lives.

For a first-party web application with a browser client, a plain session cookie
remains the simplest correct answer, and "we used JWTs because they are modern"
is the wrong reason to have a revocation problem.

## The JWT vulnerabilities, and what they have in common

Three families, all the same mistake in different clothes.

**`alg: none`.** Early libraries treated the header's algorithm as
instructions. A token claiming no algorithm was accepted with no signature.
Fixed everywhere years ago, and it still appears in home-grown verifiers.

**Algorithm confusion.** A server that verifies RS256 with a public key can be
sent a token signed with HS256 using that public key as the HMAC secret. The
library sees `alg: HS256`, looks up "the key", and verifies successfully —
because the public key is public. The fix is to pin the expected algorithm at
the call site.

**Key confusion via `kid` or `jku`.** Headers that point at *which* key to use
are attacker-controlled. A `kid` used directly as a file path or SQL fragment is
a traversal or injection; a `jku` URL fetched and trusted is a complete bypass.

The common thread is that a JWT header is data from the attacker, and every one
of these bugs comes from treating it as configuration. The one-line rule — the
verifier decides the algorithm and the key, the token is only data — makes all
three impossible.

## Cookies, and the browser rules you inherit

Cookie security is mostly a matter of knowing which attributes the browser
enforces for you. `HttpOnly` is what makes an XSS "steal data on this page"
rather than "become this user forever". `SameSite=Lax` — the default in
Chrome since 2020 — removed most CSRF from the web without anyone changing
their code, though it does not cover same-site subdomains, and `Lax` still
allows top-level GET navigation, which is why a state-changing GET remains a
bad idea.

The `__Host-` prefix is a small, elegant piece of design worth knowing. A
browser refuses to store a cookie whose name starts with `__Host-` unless it is
`Secure`, has `Path=/` and has *no* `Domain` attribute. That last requirement
is the point: without it, a compromised `blog.example.com` can set a cookie for
`example.com`, and your main application cannot tell it apart from its own.
The prefix turns a convention you must remember into a rule the browser
enforces.

CSRF defence beyond `SameSite` is the double-submit pattern: a random value in
a non-`HttpOnly` cookie and the same value in a header, compared server-side.
It works because a cross-site attacker can cause the cookie to be *sent* but
cannot *read* it to populate the header. The signed variant binds the token to
the session so it cannot be transplanted.

## Where this goes next

Everything here is per-request work: a lookup, a hash comparison, a signature
verify. That makes it a natural place for the concerns of the next sectors —
caching an authorization decision, rate limiting by identity rather than by IP,
and making sure a slow identity provider cannot take your service down with it.
Authentication is also the layer people forget to include in a graceful
shutdown: a session store connection is a resource, and closing it before
in-flight requests finish produces 500s on exactly the requests users notice.

## The status codes, and what a client does with them

`401` and `403` are not two shades of "no". A client that receives 401 is
supposed to acquire credentials and try again; a client that receives 403 is
supposed to stop. Sending 401 for a permission failure therefore produces a
retry loop — the client refreshes its perfectly valid token, presents it again,
and is refused again — and the symptom is a support ticket about your API
"rate limiting" someone.

The 401 must carry `WWW-Authenticate`. It is a MUST in RFC 9110, it names the
scheme the client should use, and almost nobody sends it. RFC 6750 extends it
with `error` and `error_description` parameters for bearer tokens, and puts
`insufficient_scope` on a **403** rather than a 401 — a detail worth knowing
because it is the one case where a permission failure still carries a
challenge, telling the client which scope to ask for next time.

The other recurring argument is 403 versus 404 for a resource the caller may
not see. 403 is honest and confirms the resource exists; 404 hides existence
and confuses legitimate users. The workable rule is to use 403 when the
identifier is not sensitive and 404 when enumerability is the risk — and above
all to be consistent, because an inconsistent service leaks existence through
the difference between its two answers.

## When not to build it

Do not build a password login if you can avoid it. Delegating to an identity
provider — OIDC with a provider you trust, or passkeys, where the browser holds
a private key and there is no shared secret to steal — removes the entire
category of password-database incidents. Build what is in this sector when you
are the identity provider, when you are integrating something that cannot
delegate, or when you need to understand what a library is doing before you
trust it with your users.

## Problem 1 — comparing a secret, and asking for one

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Export `safeEqual`, `bearerChallenge` and
`authenticateBearer`.

`safeEqual(a, b)` compares two strings in time that does not depend on where
they differ. Use `node:crypto`; `===` is the wrong answer even when the result
is right.

`bearerChallenge({ realm, error, description })` builds a `WWW-Authenticate`
value: `Bearer realm="api"`, with `, error="invalid_token"` and
`, error_description="..."` appended when supplied, in that order. Values are
quoted, and a `"` or `\` inside a value is backslash-escaped.

`authenticateBearer(authorization, tokens)` returns
`{ ok: true; token: string }` or
`{ ok: false; status: 401; code: string; headers: Record<string, string> }`:

- header absent or empty → `code: "missing_token"`, a challenge with **no**
  `error` parameter (RFC 6750: the plain challenge invites credentials);
- present but not `Bearer <token>` — wrong scheme, no space, empty token →
  `code: "invalid_request"` and `error="invalid_request"`;
- well-formed but not in `tokens` → `code: "invalid_token"` and
  `error="invalid_token"`;
- the scheme is compared case-insensitively (`bearer` is legal), the token is
  not.
