## Hint 1

`crypto.timingSafeEqual` compares two `Buffer`s without short-circuiting, but
it **throws** when their lengths differ — which is precisely the case you meet
with a truncated token. Hash both sides to a fixed width first and the problem
disappears:

```ts
const digest = (value: string) => createHash("sha256").update(value, "utf8").digest();
return timingSafeEqual(digest(a), digest(b));
```

Both operands are now 32 bytes whatever arrived.

## Hint 2

Do not iterate `tokens` with `some(t => safeEqual(t, token))` and return early
on a match — that is a timing leak of a different kind, though a much weaker
one. Accumulate instead:

```ts
let found = false;
for (const candidate of tokens) found = safeEqual(candidate, token) || found;
```

The `|| found` ordering matters: `safeEqual` must run for every candidate, and
`found || safeEqual(...)` would short-circuit once a match is seen.

## Hint 3

The three failure branches map to three different messages *to the client*,
which is the part people skip. A 401 with no `WWW-Authenticate` is a protocol
violation and leaves a client guessing which scheme to use. The distinction
between the bare challenge and `error="invalid_token"` matters too: the first
means "you sent nothing", the second means "what you sent is no good", and a
client that retries after the second without getting a new token will loop
forever.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The timing attack is worth understanding rather than accepting on faith. String
`===` returns as soon as two bytes differ, so a token that shares the first
byte with a valid one takes measurably longer to reject than one that does not.
Feed a few thousand samples into a statistical test and you recover the token
one byte at a time. Over the public internet this is hard; from another
container on the same host it is not, and "hard" is not a security property you
control.

## Hint 2

Notice what `safeEqual` does *not* protect. The length of the input is still
observable, and the number of candidate tokens still affects total time. That
is fine: neither leaks the secret. Being able to say which parts of a
computation are secret-dependent — and only hardening those — is the actual
skill here, rather than reflexively wrapping everything in constant-time
helpers.

## Hint 3

The quoting rule in `bearerChallenge` exists because these are `quoted-string`
values in RFC 9110's grammar, and an unescaped `"` in a realm or description
truncates the header at the wrong place. Since your description may end up
containing user-influenced text, the escape is not decoration — it is the
difference between a header and a header-injection primitive.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a password hash you can live with

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Export `hashPassword`, `verifyPassword` and
`verifyLogin`.

`hashPassword(password)` returns a self-describing string:

```
scrypt$16384$8$1$<salt base64url>$<key base64url>
```

- a fresh 16-byte random salt per password;
- `scrypt` from `node:crypto` with `N=16384, r=8, p=1` and a 64-byte key;
- the password is `.normalize("NFKC")`d before hashing, so two Unicode
  spellings of the same accented characters agree;
- the parameters are part of the string, not a constant somewhere.

`verifyPassword(stored, password)` re-derives with the parameters *from the
stored string* and compares in constant time. A malformed or unknown-algorithm
`stored` returns `false` — it never throws.

`verifyLogin(record, password)` takes `record: string | undefined` (the stored
hash, or nothing when the user does not exist) and returns a boolean, doing the
**same work in both cases**: when the record is missing it must still perform a
derivation against a fixed dummy hash before returning `false`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`scrypt` is callback-based; wrap it once:

```ts
const derive = promisify(scrypt) as
  (password: string, salt: Buffer, keylen: number, options: ScryptOptions) => Promise<Buffer>;
```

The options object is where `N`, `r` and `p` go. Note that raising `N` also
raises the memory Node needs for the operation, and it will refuse with
`ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS` above its default `maxmem` — a real
deployment surprise, and the reason `maxmem` is worth knowing about before you
raise a cost parameter.

## Hint 2

Storing the parameters in the hash is what makes future migration possible:

```
scrypt$16384$8$1$salt$key
 ^alg   ^N   ^r ^p
```

When you raise the cost in two years, old hashes still verify with their own
parameters, and you re-hash opportunistically at the next successful login.
A codebase with `N` as a module constant has to invalidate every password to
change it, which means it never changes.

## Hint 3

`verifyLogin` is the user-enumeration defence and the shape is deliberate:

```ts
const target = record ?? DUMMY;
const ok = await verifyPassword(target, password);
return record !== undefined && ok;
```

`DUMMY` is a real hash of a random string, generated once at module load, so
the missing-user path costs the same scrypt derivation as the found-user path.
Returning `false` early instead makes login-time differences visible, and a
list of which email addresses have accounts is exactly what a credential
stuffer wants next.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason for slowness, in one sentence: your server hashes once per login, an
attacker with your database hashes once per guess, so the cost parameter sets
the exchange rate between your latency budget and their guessing rate. A
100-millisecond hash is invisible to a user and reduces an offline attack from
billions of guesses per second to ten.

## Hint 2

Do not trim, lowercase, or length-cap the password on the way in. Each of those
shrinks the keyspace, and trimming in particular produces the worst kind of
bug: a user whose password manager pastes a trailing space can log in on the
device that trims and not on the one that does not. Normalise Unicode, because
that is about two byte sequences meaning the same character, and change nothing
else.

## Hint 3

`verifyPassword` returning `false` for malformed input rather than throwing is
a deliberate boundary decision. The stored string comes from your database and
should always be well-formed — but "should" plus a partial migration equals a
500 on the login endpoint at three in the morning. Failing closed (deny, log,
carry on) is the right behaviour for an authentication check that meets data it
does not understand.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — a signed cookie, and rotating the key that signs it

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Export `createSigner(keys)` where `keys` is a non-empty
array of `{ id: string; secret: string }`, newest first, returning
`{ sign, unsign }`.

`sign(value)` produces `<kid>.<payload>.<mac>`:

- `payload` is the value base64url-encoded, so a value containing `.` cannot
  break the format;
- `mac` is `HMAC-SHA256` over the string `` `${kid}.${payload}` ``, base64url;
- signing always uses `keys[0]`.

`unsign(token)` returns `{ ok: true; value: string; kid: string }` or
`{ ok: false; reason }` with `reason` one of `"malformed"` (not three
non-empty parts), `"unknown_key"` (the kid is not in the ring), or
`"bad_signature"` (constant-time comparison failed). Verification uses the key
named by the token's `kid` — and only that key.

An empty key ring is a `TypeError` at `createSigner` time.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Encoding the payload is not decoration. If the value can contain a `.` and your
format is dot-separated, `split(".")` gives you the wrong pieces and the MAC
check fails for legitimate values — or, worse, an attacker chooses a value that
re-splits into a shape you accept. base64url has no `.`, no `+`, no `/` and no
padding, which is exactly why JWTs use it.

## Hint 2

Include the key id *inside* the signed material:

```ts
const mac = createHmac("sha256", key.secret).update(`${kid}.${payload}`).digest("base64url");
```

If you sign only the payload, an attacker can relabel a token with a different
`kid` and it still verifies under whichever key that names — harmless with one
ring, not harmless when one of your keys is shared with a less trusted service.
Signing the identifier binds the token to the key that made it.

## Hint 3

Rotation is the operational point. With a ring, deploying a new key is: put it
at the front, keep the old ones, and remove the oldest a week later once no
live session was signed by it. With a single secret, changing it logs everyone
out at once. The `kid` turns verification from "try every key" into a lookup,
which also means a bad token costs one HMAC rather than five.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be clear about what a MAC does and does not do. It proves the value was
produced by someone holding the key and has not been altered. It does **not**
hide the value — base64url is encoding, not encryption, and anyone can read the
payload. A signed cookie is therefore fine for a session id or a user id, and
wrong for anything the user should not see.

## Hint 2

The three failure reasons exist so the caller can log usefully while telling
the client nothing. `malformed` is usually a truncated cookie or a client bug;
`unknown_key` usually means you retired a key too early, and a spike in it
during a deploy is a signal worth alerting on; `bad_signature` is either
tampering or a key mismatch between instances. All three produce the same 401
to the user, and three different lines in your logs.

## Hint 3

Constant-time comparison applies to the MAC too, and here `timingSafeEqual` on
the decoded buffers works directly because both are 32 bytes — but only if you
check the length first, since `Buffer.from(garbage, "base64url")` happily
returns a short buffer rather than throwing. A length check followed by
`timingSafeEqual` is the safe pair; `timingSafeEqual` alone throws on the
malformed input an attacker can send for free.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — the attributes are the security

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Export `serializeCookie(name, value, attributes)` and
`parseCookies(header)`.

`serializeCookie` builds a `Set-Cookie` value. Attributes are emitted in this
order when present: `Max-Age`, `Expires`, `Domain`, `Path`, `Secure`,
`HttpOnly`, `SameSite`. Values are percent-encoded; names must match
`/^[A-Za-z0-9!#$%&'*+\-.^_`|~]+$/` or it is a `TypeError`.

The rules that make it a security feature rather than a formatter — each a
`TypeError`, because they are your mistakes, not a client's:

- `SameSite: "None"` without `Secure` is refused (browsers reject it too, and
  the failure is otherwise silent);
- a name starting with `__Host-` requires `Secure`, `Path: "/"` and **no**
  `Domain`;
- a name starting with `__Secure-` requires `Secure`;
- `maxAge` must be an integer if given; `expires` must be a valid `Date` and is
  emitted as a UTC string.

`parseCookies(header)` turns a `Cookie` header into `Record<string, string>`:
split on `;`, split each pair at the **first** `=`, trim, percent-decode the
value, drop pairs with an empty name or an undecodable value, and keep the
**first** occurrence of a repeated name.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the prefix rules as a small block at the top, before any string building.
They are the interesting part of the exercise: `__Host-` is not a naming
convention, it is a contract the browser enforces, and a cookie that violates
it is silently *not stored* — which presents as "login works locally and not in
staging" with nothing in any log.

## Hint 2

Why `__Host-` forbids `Domain`: without it, a cookie set by
`blog.example.com` for `Domain=example.com` is sent to `app.example.com`, and
your application cannot distinguish it from one it set itself. That is session
fixation via a compromised sibling subdomain, and it is why the prefix bundles
"no Domain", "Path=/" and "Secure" into one enforceable rule.

## Hint 3

`parseCookies` taking the **first** occurrence is a deliberate choice and worth
knowing the reason for. Browsers may send two cookies with the same name and
different paths, and different servers pick differently — which is the basis of
cookie-shadowing attacks. Picking the first, documenting it, and preferring
`__Host-` names (which cannot be shadowed by a subdomain) is the defensible
combination.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Go through the attributes asking "which attack does this stop?" — `HttpOnly`
turns an XSS from account takeover into data theft on one page; `Secure` stops
a downgrade to plaintext; `SameSite=Lax` removes most CSRF; `Max-Age` bounds a
stolen cookie's usefulness. If you cannot name the attack, you will eventually
omit the attribute during a refactor, because it looks like noise.

## Hint 2

`SameSite=Lax` versus `Strict` is a product decision, not a security maximum.
`Strict` withholds the cookie even on top-level navigation, so a user following
a link from their email lands logged out — which trains people to think your
app is broken. `Lax` sends it on top-level GET navigation only, which is safe
provided you have no state-changing GET endpoints. That proviso is the real
requirement hiding inside the choice.

## Hint 3

Percent-encoding the value matters because cookie values may not contain
commas, semicolons or whitespace. Encode on the way out and decode on the way
in, and note that `decodeURIComponent` throws on `%zz` — which an attacker can
send for free, so the parser must catch it and drop the pair rather than
turning a malformed cookie into a 500 on every request that carries it.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The order of the checks is the exercise. Signature before claims, always: a
token whose signature you have not verified is a string an attacker wrote, and
reading `exp` from it to decide anything — including which error to return — is
trusting it. The only field you may read before verifying is `alg`, and you
read it in order to *reject* it.

## Hint 2

The rule that prevents every famous JWT vulnerability, stated as code:

```ts
if (header.alg !== "HS256") return { ok: false, code: "unexpected_alg" };
```

Not `switch (header.alg)`, not a lookup table keyed by the token's value. The
verifier decides the algorithm; the token is data. `alg: none` and the
RS256-to-HS256 confusion attack both work by persuading a library to take
instructions from the thing it is checking.

## Hint 3

Skew exists because clocks disagree. A token issued by a machine 30 seconds
ahead of yours is `nbf`-invalid the instant it is created if you allow no
tolerance, and the resulting bug is intermittent, environment-specific and
maddening. Sixty seconds is the conventional allowance, applied in both
directions: `exp + skew` and `nbf - skew`.

Missing `exp` being an error rather than "never expires" is the other
deliberate strictness — an unexpiring bearer token is a permanent credential
that you cannot revoke.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Note what a JWT is *not*: it is signed, not encrypted. Anyone with the token
can read the payload — `atob` in a browser console is enough. Every claim you
put in one is public to the holder, which rules out internal identifiers you
would not show a user, and makes "we store the permissions in the token"
a decision about disclosure as well as staleness.

## Hint 2

The `kid` header is where implementations reintroduce the vulnerability they
just closed. It is attacker-controlled data, so using it directly as a file
path, a database query fragment, or a URL to fetch turns it into traversal,
injection or full bypass. Treat it as a lookup key into a map you control, and
treat an unknown value as a rejection rather than a fallback to "the default
key".

## Hint 3

An architectural point worth carrying: everything a JWT knows was true when it
was issued. If a user's role changes, or they are banned, or a session is
logged out, the token does not know. Short lifetimes (five to fifteen minutes)
are the standard mitigation, which means a refresh mechanism, which means
server state after all — the trade the next exercise makes explicit.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — sessions, fixation, and two kinds of expiry

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Export
`createSessionStore({ now, newId, idleMs, absoluteMs })` returning
`{ start, get, touch, destroy, sweep, size }`.

- `start(userId, previousId?)` creates a session with a **new** id, records
  `createdAt` and `lastSeenAt` as `now()`, destroys `previousId` if given, and
  returns the new id. Rotating the id at every login is the whole session
  fixation defence.
- `get(id)` returns `{ userId, createdAt, lastSeenAt }` or `null`. A session
  past **either** deadline is deleted and reported as `null`.
- `touch(id)` is `get` plus sliding the idle window: `lastSeenAt = now()`. It
  must **not** move `createdAt`, so the absolute deadline is unaffected.
- `destroy(id)` removes it, returning whether anything was there.
- `sweep()` removes every expired session and returns how many it removed.
- `size()` is the current count.

Deadlines: idle is `lastSeenAt + idleMs`, absolute is `createdAt + absoluteMs`,
and a session is expired when `now()` is **greater than or equal to** either.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One private `expired(session)` predicate used by `get`, `touch` and `sweep` is
what keeps the two deadlines consistent. Every implementation that inlines the
comparison ends up with three subtly different versions, and the one in
`sweep` is the one nobody tests.

## Hint 2

The fixation defence is a single line and worth stating precisely: the id after
login must never be the id before it. If an attacker can plant a session id on
a victim — via a URL parameter, a cookie set by a sibling subdomain, or an XSS —
and you keep that id through login, the attacker's copy is now an
authenticated session. Issuing a new id at every privilege change closes it,
which is why `start` takes `previousId` and destroys it.

## Hint 3

`touch` moving `lastSeenAt` but not `createdAt` is the crux of having two
deadlines. Idle expiry logs out an abandoned laptop; absolute expiry bounds the
damage of a stolen cookie no matter how actively it is used. An implementation
that slides both has only one deadline, and it is the weaker one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what each deadline defends against and the design stops being arbitrary.
Idle: the user walked away. Absolute: someone else has the cookie and is using
it constantly, so the idle timer never fires. A system with only idle expiry
gives a thief an indefinite session; a system with only absolute expiry leaves
a public-terminal session live for hours.

## Hint 2

Note the deliberate `>=` in the expiry comparison. Boundary conditions in
time-based code are where injected clocks earn their keep: the gate can set
`now` to exactly `createdAt + absoluteMs` and assert the session is gone.
Real code that used `>` would be correct in production and untestable at the
boundary, which is a small but real reason to specify the comparison.

## Hint 3

`sweep` exists because expiry-on-access alone leaks memory: sessions nobody
touches again stay in the map forever. In a real deployment this is a periodic
timer (`setInterval(...).unref()`, so it does not hold the process open — the
last sector of this volume returns to that) or a TTL in Redis. Returning the
count makes it a metric, and a sweep count that suddenly jumps is a useful
signal about traffic shape.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — refresh tokens, rotation, and what reuse means

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Export
`createRefreshStore({ now, newToken, ttlMs })` returning
`{ issue, rotate, revokeFamily, size }`.

- Tokens are stored **hashed** (SHA-256, hex) — the store must never hold a
  usable token, so that a database dump is not a set of live credentials.
- `issue(userId)` mints a token in a new family and returns
  `{ token, familyId }`.
- `rotate(token)` is the whole exercise:
  - unknown hash → `{ ok: false, reason: "unknown" }`;
  - the family has been revoked → `{ ok: false, reason: "revoked" }`;
  - the token was already rotated once → **reuse detected**: revoke the entire
    family and return `{ ok: false, reason: "reuse_detected", familyId }`;
  - past `ttlMs` since it was issued → `{ ok: false, reason: "expired" }`;
  - otherwise mark it used and return `{ ok: true, token, familyId }` with a
    fresh token in the same family.
- `revokeFamily(familyId)` returns whether it existed.
- `size()` is the number of stored token records.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two maps make this readable: token hash → record, and family id → revoked
flag. Trying to hold it in one structure produces a lookup that has to scan.
Note that the token hash is the key — `issue` returns the plaintext once and
then forgets it, which is the same discipline as a password hash.

## Hint 2

The reuse rule is the part worth understanding rather than implementing from
the spec. A refresh token is single-use. If an old one is presented again there
are exactly two explanations: the legitimate client never received the response
containing its replacement (a dropped connection), or someone else has a copy.
You cannot tell which from the request, so you assume the worse one and revoke
the family. The legitimate user is logged out and re-authenticates; the thief
is locked out. That asymmetry is why the rule is worth its false positives.

## Hint 3

Order the checks deliberately: revoked before used before expired. A token from
a revoked family that is also expired should report `revoked`, because that is
the fact an operator needs when reading the logs. And reuse detection must come
before the expiry check, or a thief can wait out the TTL and get a quieter
error than the alarm you wanted.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the design OAuth 2's Security Best Current Practice recommends for
public clients — browsers and mobile apps, which cannot keep a secret. The
whole scheme exists because such a client must hold a long-lived credential
somewhere an attacker might reach, so the mitigation is not "make it
unstealable" but "make theft detectable". Rotation plus reuse detection is that
detection mechanism.

## Hint 2

Hashing tokens at rest deserves the same argument as passwords, with one
difference: a refresh token is high-entropy random, so it needs no salt and no
slow KDF. A single SHA-256 is enough, because there is no dictionary to attack.
Using scrypt here would be a hundred times slower for no gain — knowing *why*
the two cases differ is more useful than either rule alone.

## Hint 3

A practical consideration the exercise leaves out: the dropped-response case is
real and users hit it. Production systems soften it with a short grace window —
a rotated token stays valid for a few seconds so a retried request succeeds —
at the cost of a small window where a stolen token also works. Being able to
name that trade, and to say you would rather log a user out than miss a theft,
is the answer an interviewer is looking for.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The ordering encodes a rule you can state in words: identity before
permission, permission before ownership. Checking ownership first would leak
whether a record exists to someone with no permission to know, which is the
subtle information disclosure inside every "403 versus 404" argument.

## Hint 2

Fail closed on an unknown action is the single most valuable line here. The
alternative — allow what has no policy — means every new endpoint is public
until someone remembers to write a rule, and the gap is invisible in code
review because the missing thing is missing. Deny by default makes the omission
loud: the endpoint returns 403 in the first test anyone writes.

## Hint 3

The broken-access-control bug this exercise is built around is worth naming
directly: an endpoint that verifies the caller is logged in and then loads
`orders/:id` without checking who owns it. It has topped the OWASP list for
years, it is invisible to a scanner, and it is why `ownership` is a policy flag
rather than something each handler remembers to do.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Scopes and roles answer different questions and both are here on purpose. A
scope is what the *client application* was authorised to do on the user's
behalf ("this app may read your orders"). A role is what the *user* is allowed
to do ("this user is a support agent"). A support agent using an app that was
only granted read access should not be able to write, which is why both checks
run and neither substitutes for the other.

## Hint 2

The `admin` bypass is deliberately narrow: it skips ownership only, not scope
and not roles. A broad "admins can do anything" branch placed at the top is how
an admin token with a read-only scope ends up deleting things. Keep the bypass
adjacent to the rule it relaxes.

## Hint 3

On 403 versus 404 for a resource you may not see: 403 is honest and leaks
existence; 404 hides existence and confuses legitimate users. The usual rule is
403 when the resource identifier is not sensitive (an order number the user
already knows), 404 when enumerability is the risk (a document id in a shared
namespace). Decide per resource, write it down, and be consistent — an
inconsistent service leaks existence through the difference.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a login that holds together

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createAuthApp(deps)` returns a `node:http`
handler implementing a cookie session with a CSRF defence. `deps` supplies
`users` (a `Map` from email to `{ id, hash }`), `verifyLogin`, `sign`/`unsign`
(the ex3 signer), `newId`, `newCsrf` and `now`.

Endpoints:

- **`POST /login`** — JSON `{ email, password }`. On success: start a session
  with a **new** id (destroying any session the request already carried), and
  set two cookies on one response —
  `__Host-sid` = the signed session id, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `Path=/`,
  `SameSite=Lax`, `Max-Age=1800`; and `__Host-csrf` = a fresh random value,
  **not** `HttpOnly`, otherwise the same attributes. Answer `204`.
  On failure: `401`, body `{"error":"invalid_credentials"}` — identical for an
  unknown email and a wrong password, and taking the same work either way.
- **`GET /me`** — valid session → `200 {"userId":"..."}`; otherwise `401` with
  `www-authenticate: Cookie realm="api"`.
- **`POST /profile`** — requires a valid session **and** a `x-csrf-token`
  header equal to the `__Host-csrf` cookie, compared in constant time.
  Missing or mismatched → `403 {"error":"csrf_failed"}`. Success → `204`.
- **`POST /logout`** — destroys the session and clears both cookies with
  `Max-Age=0`; `204` whether or not a session was found.

Every response sets `cache-control: no-store` — an authenticated response in a
shared cache is a data leak.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb04_auth_sessions_tokens challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the cookie work in one place. A helper that reads the request's cookies,
unsigns the session id, and returns `{ session, csrf }` gives every route the
same view, and a second helper that sets or clears the pair keeps the
attributes from drifting between login and logout — a mismatch there means the
logout does not actually clear the cookie, because a `Set-Cookie` only replaces
one with the same name, path and domain.

## Hint 2

Double-submit CSRF works because of an asymmetry in what a cross-site attacker
can do: they can cause the browser to *send* your cookies, but they cannot
*read* them, so they cannot copy the value into a header. That is also why the
CSRF cookie must not be `HttpOnly` — your own JavaScript has to read it — and
why the session cookie must be.

## Hint 3

Three things the gate will check that are easy to skip:

- the session id after a login is different from any id sent with the login
  request (fixation);
- the two `Set-Cookie` headers arrive as two values, not one joined string —
  `appendHeader`, or an array, from sector 1;
- the failure response for an unknown email is byte-identical to the one for a
  wrong password, and both do the same hashing work.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the failure path first. Login endpoints are graded on what they refuse to
tell you: no distinction between unknown and wrong, no timing difference, no
detail in the body, and nothing in the response that varies with the input.
Once that is right, the success path is bookkeeping.

## Hint 2

`cache-control: no-store` on every response is not paranoia. A shared cache — a
corporate proxy, a CDN misconfiguration, a browser's back-forward cache — that
retains `GET /me` will hand one user's identity to another. `no-store` is the
strong form (do not write it down anywhere); `private, no-cache` permits a
browser-only copy with revalidation, which is sometimes what you want for a
personalised page but not for an identity endpoint.

## Hint 3

Constant-time comparison for the CSRF token surprises people, since the value
is not exactly a secret — the client is expected to read it. Use it anyway: it
costs nothing, and the general rule "any comparison that gates access is
constant time" is much easier to apply consistently than a case-by-case
judgement about which secrets are secret enough.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — reading the credential off the wire

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Export `parseAuthorization(header)` returning a
discriminated union or `null`:

```ts
type Credentials =
  | { scheme: "basic"; user: string; password: string }
  | { scheme: "bearer"; token: string }
  | { scheme: "other"; name: string; parameters: string };
```

- The scheme name is matched case-insensitively and reported lowercased for
  `basic` and `bearer`; for anything else, `name` keeps the spelling that
  arrived.
- One or more spaces may separate the scheme from the rest; leading and
  trailing whitespace is ignored.
- `Basic` decodes base64 and splits at the **first** colon; the username may
  not contain a colon, the password may contain any number. Bytes are decoded
  as UTF-8 (RFC 7617's `charset` parameter). No colon at all, or input that is
  not valid base64, is `null`.
- `Bearer` accepts only the `token68` character set
  (`A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ + /` with optional `=` padding); anything else is
  `null`.
- A header with no scheme, or a scheme with no parameters, is `null`.

## Hint 1

Split once, on the first run of whitespace, and keep the remainder verbatim:

```ts
const match = /^\s*(\S+)\s+(.*?)\s*$/.exec(header);
```

Do not `split(" ")` — a `Basic` credential's base64 never contains a space, but
an `other` scheme's parameters routinely do (`Digest username="x", realm="y"`),
and joining them back together after splitting is how a parser starts losing
information.

## Hint 2

Base64 validation in Node is easy to get wrong because `Buffer.from(x,
"base64")` never throws: it ignores characters it does not recognise and
returns whatever it managed. Re-encode and compare, or test the string against
`/^[A-Za-z0-9+/]+={0,2}$/` with a length check, before trusting the decode.
Otherwise `Basic ###` parses as an empty credential.

## Hint 3

Splitting at the **first** colon is required by RFC 7617 and is a genuine trap:
`user:pa:ss` is the user `user` with password `pa:ss`, not an error. Use
`indexOf(":")` and two `slice`s. A `split(":")` with destructuring silently
truncates the password at the first colon, which produces an authentication
failure for exactly the users with the strongest passwords.

## Hint 1

Ask why this parse deserves its own function at all. Because it runs before
every authorization decision on every request, and because the failure mode of
being sloppy is silent: a token you truncated is a token that fails to match,
which looks like an expired credential and sends the client into a refresh loop
you will spend an afternoon reading.

## Hint 2

The `token68` restriction on `Bearer` is worth enforcing rather than accepting
anything. It bounds what can reach your token verifier — no spaces, no quotes,
no control characters — which means a malformed `Authorization` header cannot
smuggle content into a log line, a cache key, or an upstream request you build
from it. Validating at the parse boundary is cheaper than sanitising at every
use.

## Hint 3

Note what this function deliberately does not do: no lookups, no verification,
no I/O. It turns bytes into a shape. Keeping parsing separate from deciding is
what lets you unit-test the nasty inputs — empty schemes, double spaces,
invalid base64, a colon-free Basic credential — without constructing a request
or a user database, and it is the same separation the router in sector 2 made
between matching and handling.

# V3·NB5 — Caching, ETags and conditional requests

Caching is the cheapest performance work available and the easiest to get
subtly wrong, because a cache bug does not look like a bug. It looks like a
user seeing yesterday's price, one customer seeing another's dashboard, or a
deploy that "did not take" for forty minutes. None of those produce an error,
and none of them reproduce on your machine.

You have already met one piece of this: `d18_http_raw` had you answer a
conditional GET and refuse a stale write with `If-Match`. This sector is the
whole model — who may store a response, for how long, how a client asks "has it
changed?", and what a well-behaved server does with the answer.

## Four questions, four groups of headers

**May this be stored, and by whom?** `Cache-Control` with `public`, `private`,
`no-store` and `no-cache`. The word that misleads everyone is `no-cache`: it
does not mean "do not cache", it means "cache it, but revalidate before every
reuse". `no-store` is the one that means what people think `no-cache` means.
`private` means a browser may keep it but a shared cache — a CDN, a corporate
proxy — may not, which is the header standing between a personalised page and a
data leak.

**For how long?** `max-age` in seconds, `s-maxage` overriding it for shared
caches, and the `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` extensions that
let a cache serve a slightly old copy while it fetches a new one, or when the
origin is down. The old `Expires` header is an absolute date and loses to
`max-age` whenever both are present; it survives only for HTTP/1.0 clients that
no longer exist.

**How does a client check?** Validators. An `ETag` is an opaque string you
choose — usually a hash of the bytes — and `Last-Modified` is a timestamp with
one-second resolution. The client sends them back as `If-None-Match` and
`If-Modified-Since`, and a match earns a `304 Not Modified` with no body. This
is the single highest-value caching feature for an API, because it turns a
50 KB JSON response into a 200-byte header exchange without giving up
freshness at all.

**Which stored copy applies?** `Vary`. A cache keys on the URL plus the request
headers named in `Vary`. Omit `Vary: Accept-Encoding` and a proxy may hand
gzipped bytes to a client that did not ask for them. Omit
`Vary: Authorization` on a personalised response and the cache hands one user's
data to another — which is why `private` matters even when you think nothing is
in front of you.

## Strong and weak, and why the distinction exists

A **strong** validator changes whenever the bytes change: a hash of the body
qualifies. A **weak** validator, written `W/"abc"`, changes only when the
*meaning* changes — two responses that differ in an embedded timestamp or in
whitespace may share one. `Last-Modified` is inherently weak at
sub-second resolution, because two edits in the same second are
indistinguishable.

The distinction is not academic. Range requests (`If-Range`) require a strong
validator, because assembling a file from pieces produced by different versions
is corruption. Conditional GET (`If-None-Match`) uses *weak* comparison, so
`W/"abc"` and `"abc"` match. Conditional writes (`If-Match`) use *strong*
comparison, because "the thing I read is still what is there" has to mean the
exact bytes.

## Preconditions have a mandated order

`If-Match`, `If-Unmodified-Since`, `If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since` and
`If-Range` can arrive together, and RFC 9110 §13.2.2 specifies exactly which
wins. Evaluate them in a different order and you can answer 304 to a request
that should have been 412, which means a client's write silently becomes a
no-op. Exercise 5 is that algorithm, written out, and it is the kind of thing
that is tedious once and free forever.

## Conditional writes are the other half

Validators are usually introduced as a bandwidth optimisation, which
undersells them. The same headers, pointed at a write, give you optimistic
concurrency control: two clients read a document, both edit, both save, and
without a precondition the second save silently destroys the first with no
error anywhere. `If-Match: "<etag>"` makes the write conditional on the version
the client read — a stale one is refused with `412 Precondition Failed`, the
client re-reads, merges and retries.

`428 Precondition Required` completes it by letting the server *demand* the
condition instead of merely accepting one. An API that answers 428 to an
unconditional `PUT` has made lost updates impossible rather than preventable,
which is a much stronger property than a paragraph in the documentation asking
clients to be careful.

## And a cache of your own

The last third of the sector builds an in-process response cache: TTL,
stale-while-revalidate, and single-flight — the property that a hundred
simultaneous misses for the same key produce one upstream call rather than a
hundred. That last one is the difference between a cache that protects a
backend and a cache that amplifies a thundering herd into an outage the moment
a hot key expires.

A warning about the order of the work, because it decides how much of this is
worth doing: the hardest question in caching is not which header to send, it is
*how stale is acceptable for this data*. Prices, maybe five seconds. A
published article, a day. A user's own dashboard, never. That is a product
decision wearing an engineering costume, and the headers in this sector are
only the vocabulary for writing the answer down — which is why an endpoint with
thoughtful `Cache-Control` and no ETags usually beats one with elaborate
validators and a lifetime nobody chose.

Eight problems, a challenge that assembles a caching layer, and a review on
which responses a shared cache is even allowed to store.

# Reading - node/v3nb05_caching_etags

Notes on validators, freshness, the precondition algorithm, and the ways a
cache turns into a correctness bug.

## Notes

**An ETag is opaque and must be quoted.** `"33a64df5"` is an ETag;
`33a64df5` is a syntax error that some caches will discard silently. The
content is yours to choose — a hash, a version number, a revision id — and the
client must never interpret it. A hash of the serialised body is the default
because it is automatically correct: the validator changes exactly when the
representation does.

**Weak comparison is the default for GET.** Two validators match weakly if
their opaque parts are equal, ignoring a `W/` prefix on either side. They match
strongly only if neither is weak and both are byte-equal. `If-None-Match` uses
weak; `If-Match` and `If-Range` use strong. Implementing one comparison
function with a flag is the cheapest way to keep this straight.

**`If-None-Match` beats `If-Modified-Since`.** When both are present, the
entity tag wins and the date is ignored entirely — it exists as a fallback for
clients that have no tag. Evaluating both and requiring both to pass is a
common bug that produces unnecessary 200s and no error message.

**A 304 is a header-only response with specific contents.** It must carry the
validators (`ETag`, `Last-Modified`) and any headers that would affect caching
(`Cache-Control`, `Vary`, `Expires`). It must **not** carry `Content-Length` or
`Content-Type` for a body it does not have. And it is not an error: a client
sees a 304 and uses the copy it already had.

**HTTP dates are one-second resolution, in GMT, in one format.**
`Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT` — the IMF-fixdate form. `Date.prototype.
toUTCString()` produces exactly it. The consequence of one-second resolution
is that a resource modified twice in the same second is indistinguishable to
`If-Modified-Since`, which is why `Last-Modified` is a weak validator and why
an ETag is worth the extra work.

**`Last-Modified` must be truncated to whole seconds before comparing.** A
stored timestamp of `12:00:00.500` compared against a header of `12:00:00`
reads as newer, so the server answers 200 forever and the cache never works.
Floor both sides to seconds.

**`Vary` is a cache key, not a hint.** The key is the URL plus the values of
the listed request headers. `Vary: *` means "never reusable" — the practical
equivalent of `no-store` for shared caches. Every header you list multiplies
the number of stored variants, so `Vary: User-Agent` is close to disabling
caching entirely, which is why it is a mistake rather than a precaution.

**`Authorization` makes a response uncacheable by shared caches by default.**
RFC 9111 §3.5: a shared cache must not store a response to a request carrying
`Authorization` unless the response explicitly allows it (`public`,
`s-maxage`, `must-revalidate`). This rule has saved a lot of people from
themselves, and it is why `private` plus an explicit `Vary` is the safe pattern
for personalised content rather than a belt-and-braces gesture.

**`stale-while-revalidate` is the single best caching header for an API.** It
lets a cache serve a stale copy immediately while it fetches a fresh one in the
background, so a hot key's expiry costs nobody any latency. `stale-if-error`
does the same when the origin fails, turning a five-minute outage into a
five-minute period of slightly old data.

**Single-flight is not optional at scale.** When a popular key expires, every
concurrent request misses at once and every one of them calls the upstream.
That is a thundering herd, and it takes down the backend the cache was
protecting. Storing the in-flight *promise* in the map — not just the result —
collapses them into one call, and it is about six lines.

**Invalidation is best made structural.** If the ETag is a hash of the current
representation, and the cache key includes it, nothing has to remember to purge:
a write changes the bytes, which changes the hash, which changes the key. The
caches that are hardest to reason about are the ones with an explicit
`invalidate()` that somebody has to call from the right places.

**A response with no cache headers is not uncached.** It is storable if it has
a validator, and a cache may then invent a *heuristic* lifetime — commonly a
tenth of the time since `Last-Modified`. So an endpoint you never thought about
has been making a caching decision on your behalf, chosen by someone else's
proxy. `no-store` or an explicit `max-age` is how you take that decision back,
and "we did not set any cache headers" is not a statement about behaviour.

**`Age` matters in a chain.** It tells the next cache how much of the freshness
lifetime has already been consumed. Without it, every cache in a chain restarts
the clock and a `max-age=60` response can survive for minutes. It is one line —
`Math.floor((now - storedAt) / 1000)` — and it is the difference between a
predictable and an unbounded staleness.

**An unsafe method invalidates the cached response for its URI.** RFC 9111
requires it, and the reason is immediate: a client that `PUT`s and then `GET`s
must not be handed the version it just replaced. In your own cache that means
dropping every variant keyed under that path, which is an argument for storing
the path alongside the entry rather than parsing it back out of the key.

## What each exercise is really testing

`ex1` is validators and the two comparison rules. `ex2` is conditional GET, end
to end. `ex3` is `Cache-Control` as data. `ex4` is `Vary` as a key function.
`ex5` is the precondition order. `ex6` is your own store, with the two
properties that matter under load. `ex7` is dates, where the bug is silent.
`ex8` is writes and invalidation. The challenge is a caching layer; the review
is the storability rules a shared cache follows.

# V3·NB5 — Caching, ETags and conditional requests (archive)

## The model in one diagram

```
  client ──▶ [ browser cache ] ──▶ [ shared cache / CDN ] ──▶ origin
             private, max-age        public, s-maxage           ETag
             If-None-Match           Vary: <headers>            Last-Modified
```

Four questions decide everything: may it be stored (`no-store`, `private`), for
how long (`max-age`, `s-maxage`), how do we check (`ETag`, `Last-Modified`),
and which stored copy applies (`Vary`).

## Validators

```ts
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

export const strongEtag = (body: Buffer): string =>
  `"${createHash("sha1").update(body).digest("base64url")}"`;

export const weakEtag = (version: number, size: number): string =>
  `W/"${version}-${size}"`;

export function etagMatches(a: string, b: string, strong: boolean): boolean {
  const weakA = a.startsWith("W/");
  const weakB = b.startsWith("W/");
  if (strong && (weakA || weakB)) return false;      // strong comparison
  return a.replace(/^W\//, "") === b.replace(/^W\//, "");
}
```

Strong comparison is required by `If-Match` and `If-Range`; weak comparison is
what `If-None-Match` uses. One function with a flag keeps the two rules from
drifting apart in six call sites.

## Conditional GET

```ts
const etag = strongEtag(body);
if (ifNoneMatch(req.headers["if-none-match"], etag)) {
  res.writeHead(304, { etag, "cache-control": cc, vary: "accept-encoding" });
  res.end();
  return;
}
res.writeHead(200, { etag, "cache-control": cc, "content-type": ct,
                     "content-length": body.length });
res.end(body);
```

Common mistakes:

- **`content-length: 0` on the 304.** It describes a body that does not exist;
  omit it entirely.
- **Dropping `Cache-Control` from the 304.** The client stores the new freshness
  information alongside its existing copy; without it, the copy reverts to
  heuristic freshness.
- **Evaluating `If-Modified-Since` when `If-None-Match` is present.** The tag
  wins outright.
- **An unquoted ETag.** Silently discarded by some intermediaries, so your
  conditional requests simply stop happening.

## Cache-Control, parsed and built

```ts
export function parseCacheControl(value: string): Record<string, string | true> {
  const out: Record<string, string | true> = {};
  for (const part of value.split(",")) {
    const token = part.trim();
    if (token === "") continue;
    const eq = token.indexOf("=");
    if (eq === -1) { out[token.toLowerCase()] = true; continue; }
    const name = token.slice(0, eq).trim().toLowerCase();
    out[name] = token.slice(eq + 1).trim().replace(/^"|"$/g, "");
  }
  return out;
}
```

Directive meanings that get confused, in order of how often:

| directive | what it actually means |
| --- | --- |
| `no-cache` | store it, but revalidate before every reuse |
| `no-store` | do not write it down anywhere |
| `private` | browser may store, shared caches may not |
| `public` | storable even when the request had `Authorization` |
| `max-age=n` | fresh for n seconds |
| `s-maxage=n` | as above, shared caches only, overrides `max-age` |
| `must-revalidate` | once stale, never serve without checking |
| `stale-while-revalidate=n` | serve stale for n seconds while refreshing |
| `immutable` | do not revalidate at all during freshness |

## Precondition order (RFC 9110 §13.2.2)

1. `If-Match` present → evaluate; on failure, `412`.
2. else `If-Unmodified-Since` present → evaluate; on failure, `412`.
3. `If-None-Match` present → evaluate; on failure, `304` for GET/HEAD, `412`
   otherwise.
4. else, for GET/HEAD, `If-Modified-Since` present → on failure, `304`.
5. `If-Range` with a `Range` → serve the range or the whole thing.

The word "else" in steps 2 and 4 is the part that produces bugs when it is
missed: a request carrying both `If-Match` and `If-Unmodified-Since` evaluates
only the first.

## A store worth having

```ts
async function get(key: string, load: () => Promise<Value>): Promise<Value> {
  const hit = entries.get(key);
  if (hit && now() < hit.freshUntil) return hit.value;
  if (hit && now() < hit.staleUntil) { void refresh(key, load); return hit.value; }
  return refresh(key, load);
}

function refresh(key: string, load: () => Promise<Value>): Promise<Value> {
  const flight = inflight.get(key);
  if (flight) return flight;                         // single-flight
  const p = load().finally(() => inflight.delete(key));
  inflight.set(key, p);
  return p;
}
```

Storing the in-flight promise is the whole of single-flight, and it is the
difference between a cache that protects the backend and one that hands it a
hundred simultaneous misses every time a hot key expires.

## Conditional writes, and the status codes that go with them

```ts
// PUT /config with If-Match
if (ifMatch === undefined) return 428;                 // demand the condition
if (!strongMatch(ifMatch, currentEtag)) return 412;    // someone else moved
apply(change);
return { status: 200, etag: nextEtag };
```

`412` is "the world moved since you read it"; the client re-reads, merges and
retries. `428` is "you did not tell me which version you were editing", and
sending it turns lost updates from a race you hope clients avoid into one the
protocol prevents.

Two more spellings worth knowing, both of which remove a check-then-act race:
`If-None-Match: *` on a `PUT` means create-only, and `If-Match: *` means
update-only. Each is a single header replacing a `GET` followed by a `PUT`,
with no window in between.

## Dates, and the second that disappears

```ts
Math.floor(lastModifiedMs / 1000) <= Math.floor(Date.parse(header) / 1000)
```

`new Date(ms).toUTCString()` emits IMF-fixdate exactly, so formatting is one
line. Parsing must additionally tolerate two obsolete forms — the RFC 850
`Sunday, 06-Nov-94 ...` spelling and the asctime `Sun Nov  6 ...` one — and
must *ignore* anything it cannot parse rather than failing the request, because
a recipient is required to.

The truncation is the bug that never announces itself. A stored timestamp with
milliseconds always compares as newer than a whole-second header, so the server
answers 200 forever, the client re-downloads every time, and no error is ever
logged. Floor both sides.

## Vary, and the key that goes wrong in two directions

```ts
const key = [
  `${method} ${pathname}${sortedSearch}`,
  ...vary.map((name) => `${name}: ${normalise(headers[name])}`),
].join("\n");
```

Too coarse a key is a correctness bug — a request receives a response built for
a different one. Too fine is a performance bug — every request misses while you
pay full storage cost. `Vary: User-Agent` is the classic too-fine case: millions
of distinct values, so effectively no caching at all.

Two normalisations pay for themselves. Sorting the query means `?a=1&b=2` and
`?b=2&a=1` share an entry. Collapsing `accept-encoding` to a sorted token list
means `gzip, deflate, br` and `br;q=1.0, gzip;q=0.8` do too — without it, each
browser's spelling is a separate stored object and the hit rate quietly
collapses.

And one detail that is easy to miss: a header that is *absent* must key
differently from one that is present and empty, or a client that sent nothing
can be handed a response stored for a client that did. A sentinel outside the
legal value range is the usual fix.

## The interview answers

*"What does `no-cache` do?"* Revalidate before reuse. `no-store` is the one
that means do not keep it.

*"Why do we need `Vary`?"* A cache keys on the URL; anything else that changes
the response must be in the key, or one request's answer is served to another.

*"Strong versus weak ETag?"* Strong changes with the bytes and is required for
range requests and conditional writes; weak changes with the meaning and is
what conditional GET compares.

*"How do you stop a thundering herd?"* Single-flight, plus
`stale-while-revalidate` so the expiry is not a cliff.

## Check yourself

1. What is the difference between `no-cache` and `no-store`?
2. Which comparison does `If-None-Match` use, and which does `If-Match` use?
3. Which headers must a 304 carry, and which must it not?
4. Why is `Last-Modified` a weak validator?
5. What happens when both `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since` are present?
6. What does `Vary: *` mean in practice?
7. Why can a shared cache usually not store a response to an authorised
   request?
8. What does `s-maxage` override, and for whom?
9. What problem does `stale-while-revalidate` solve that `max-age` cannot?
10. Why must ETags be quoted?
11. What is single-flight and which failure does it prevent?
12. Why truncate `Last-Modified` to whole seconds before comparing?
13. How does hashing the body make invalidation automatic?

# Caching on the web, and why the headers look like that

## Two generations of design

HTTP/1.0 had `Expires`: an absolute date after which a copy is stale. It works
until a client's clock is wrong, at which point content expires immediately or
never. HTTP/1.1 replaced it with `Cache-Control: max-age`, a *relative*
lifetime that needs no agreement about the current time — only about the
duration since the response was received. Every subsequent addition has been in
the `Cache-Control` family, and `Expires` survives only as a fallback for
clients that stopped existing two decades ago.

The other half of the design is validation, and it answers a different
question. Freshness says "you may reuse this without asking". Validation says
"ask, cheaply". A validator turns a 50 KB response into a 200-byte header
exchange, which is why an API with good ETags and a `max-age` of zero can still
be dramatically faster than one with neither: every request is conditional, and
almost all of them are 304s.

## What an ETag actually is

The specification is careful to say an ETag is opaque. The server chooses it,
the client echoes it, and nothing in between may interpret it. That freedom is
why implementations differ so much: nginx uses last-modified time plus content
length; some frameworks hash the body; databases often expose a row version
that maps directly onto one.

Hashing the body is the choice that is automatically correct — the validator
changes exactly when the representation changes — and its cost is that you must
have the bytes before you can produce the header, which rules it out for very
large or streamed responses. For those, a version-plus-size weak tag is the
usual compromise, and the weakness is honest: it says "this may be the same
thing" rather than "these are the same bytes".

There is one subtlety with compression. If a proxy gzips your response, the
bytes change, so the strong ETag no longer describes what the client received.
This is why the specification allows a transformed representation to weaken the
tag, and why `Vary: Accept-Encoding` matters: it puts the encoding in the cache
key so the two variants are stored separately rather than confused.

## Preconditions, and the lost update they prevent

The write-side story is the more interesting one. Two clients read a document,
both edit it, both write. Without preconditions the second write silently
overwrites the first, and the first user's change is gone with no error
anywhere. `If-Match: "<etag>"` makes the write conditional on the version they
read: the second write fails with `412 Precondition Failed`, the client
re-reads, merges, and retries. This is optimistic concurrency control, and HTTP
has had it since 1997.

`428 Precondition Required` (RFC 6585) completes the pattern by letting a
server *demand* the condition rather than accepting an unconditional write. An
API that returns 428 for a `PUT` without `If-Match` has made lost updates
impossible rather than merely preventable, which is a much stronger property.

The order of evaluation exists because the conditions are not independent. A
request with `If-Match` (a write condition) and `If-None-Match` (a read
condition) is asking two different questions, and answering the read one first
would let a stale write through as a 304. The mandated order puts the write
conditions first, and the "else" clauses ensure the entity-tag forms take
precedence over the date forms — because dates have one-second resolution and
tags do not.

## Vary, and the cache poisoning it prevents

A cache stores responses under a key. If the key is just the URL, and your
response depends on a request header, the cache will eventually serve the wrong
one. `Vary` names the headers that participate in the key, and every one you
add multiplies the stored variants — which is why `Vary: User-Agent` is close
to disabling caching (there are millions of distinct user agent strings) and
why `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is almost always the only one you need.

The security version of this is web cache poisoning: if some *unkeyed* input
influences the response — a header the cache does not vary on, a query
parameter it strips — an attacker can make a request that produces a hostile
response and gets stored under a key that innocent users will hit. The defences
are the same discipline as everywhere else in this volume: do not let inputs
you have not declared influence the output, and declare the ones that do.

## Serving stale, on purpose

`stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` (RFC 5861) are the two most
useful modern additions, because they change the shape of failure. Without
them, a cache entry's expiry is a cliff: at second 60 every request misses
simultaneously. With `stale-while-revalidate=30`, the first request after
expiry gets the old copy immediately and triggers a background refresh, so the
p99 never sees the cliff at all. With `stale-if-error=600`, an origin outage
becomes ten minutes of slightly old data instead of ten minutes of 502s.

Both are supported by CDNs and by browsers, and both encode a judgement you
should make explicitly: *how old is too old for this data?* Prices, maybe five
seconds. A blog post, a day. A user's own dashboard, never — `private,
no-store` and a fast origin.

## Single-flight, and the herd

The in-process version of the same problem has a different name. When a hot key
expires and a hundred requests arrive in the same millisecond, a naive cache
issues a hundred upstream calls. If the upstream is a database doing an
expensive aggregate, the cache has just amplified a routine expiry into an
outage — and the classic pathology is that the outage keeps the calls slow,
which keeps the key missing, which keeps the herd arriving.

The fix is to store the in-flight promise rather than only the settled value,
so the second through hundredth callers await the first one's work. It is six
lines, it composes with `stale-while-revalidate`, and it is one of the highest
value-to-effort ratios in server engineering.

## Storability, and the rule that saves people from themselves

RFC 9111 §3 lists when a shared cache may store a response at all, and one
clause has prevented more incidents than the rest combined: a response to a
request carrying `Authorization` must not be stored by a shared cache unless
the response explicitly says otherwise with `public`, `s-maxage` or
`must-revalidate`. Without it, the first CDN placed in front of an
authenticated API would serve one user's data to the next.

The rest of the list is worth reading once so you know what happens by default.
A status in the cacheable-by-default set (200, 203, 204, 300, 301, 308, 404,
405, 410, 414, 501) with a validator and no `Cache-Control` at all *is*
storable, with a heuristic lifetime. That is the sentence that surprises
people: silence is not "do not cache", it is "cache with a lifetime somebody
else chooses". Every endpoint shipped without cache headers has been making
that choice implicitly.

## When not to cache

When correctness depends on freshness and the data is cheap to fetch, a cache
is a liability with a latency benefit. When the response is personalised and
you are not certain every intermediary respects `private`. When your
invalidation story is "someone remembers to call purge" — that is not a story,
and the resulting staleness will be discovered by a customer.

And the honest general note: the hardest part of caching is not the headers,
it is deciding what may be stale and for how long. That is a product question
wearing an engineering costume, and the headers in this sector are only the
vocabulary for writing the answer down.
