exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — validators, and the two ways to compare them

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Export `strongEtag`, `weakEtag`, `parseEtagList` and
`etagMatches`.

- `strongEtag(body: Buffer)` → `"<base64url sha1 of the bytes>"`, quoted.
- `weakEtag(version: number, size: number)` → `W/"<version>-<size>"`.
- `parseEtagList(header)` → the entries of a comma-separated `If-Match` /
  `If-None-Match` header, trimmed, empties dropped, `W/` prefixes preserved.
  `undefined` gives `[]`; a header of `*` gives `["*"]`.
- `etagMatches(candidate, current, { strong })`:
  - `*` matches anything;
  - under **weak** comparison, `W/"a"` and `"a"` match — strip the prefix from
    both sides and compare the opaque parts;
  - under **strong** comparison, a `W/` on **either** side means no match, and
    the remaining comparison is byte-equal.

An unquoted candidate never matches a quoted current tag; do not "helpfully"
add quotes.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One comparison function with a boolean, not two functions. The two rules differ
in exactly one place — whether a `W/` prefix disqualifies — and writing them
separately guarantees that in six months one of them gains a fix the other does
not.

## Hint 2

Which comparison goes where is the part to memorise:

- `If-None-Match` (conditional GET) → **weak**;
- `If-Match` (conditional write) → **strong**;
- `If-Range` (partial GET) → **strong**.

The reason is what each is protecting. A GET wants "is this still the same
thing?", and a semantically equivalent representation counts. A write wants "is
this the exact version I read?", because otherwise you overwrite someone. A
range wants "may I splice these bytes together?", where any difference is
corruption.

## Hint 3

Refusing to add quotes to an unquoted candidate is deliberate. An unquoted
entity tag is a syntax error, and a client that sends one is broken; being
lenient hides the bug and creates a client that only works against your server.
Being strict here costs a client one debugging session and everyone else
nothing — the opposite trade to Postel's law, and the one modern protocol
design prefers.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with what a validator is *for*: it is an opaque token that changes when
the thing changes. Everything else follows. A hash of the body qualifies
because it changes exactly when the bytes do. A row version qualifies. A random
UUID per response does not, because it changes when nothing changed, and every
conditional request becomes a full response.

## Hint 2

Note the cost of the strong tag: you must have the complete body before you can
compute it, so it cannot be used with a streamed response of unknown length.
That is why `weakEtag(version, size)` exists in this exercise — it is derivable
from metadata, which a database row gives you for free, and it is honest about
being weak.

## Hint 3

`*` deserves a moment because it means different things on each side.
`If-None-Match: *` means "only if this does not exist" — the way to make a
`PUT` create-only. `If-Match: *` means "only if this does exist" — the way to
make a `PUT` update-only. One header, two useful contracts, and both are more
precise than a `POST` plus a duplicate check.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — the cheapest response you can send

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createHandler(load)` takes
`load(): { body: Buffer; contentType: string; version: number }` and serves
`GET`/`HEAD` on `/doc`.

- `200` carries `content-type`, an exact `content-length`, `cache-control:
  private, max-age=60`, `vary: accept-encoding`, and a strong `etag`.
- A matching `if-none-match` (weak comparison, `*` accepted) → `304` carrying
  **only** `etag`, `cache-control` and `vary` — no `content-type`, no
  `content-length`, no body.
- No `if-none-match`, but an `if-modified-since` no older than the document's
  `lastModified` (whole seconds) → `304` as above plus `last-modified`.
- When `if-none-match` is present, `if-modified-since` is **ignored entirely**,
  even if it would have produced a different answer.
- Every `200` also carries `last-modified`, formatted with `toUTCString()`.
- `HEAD` gets the `200` headers and no body.
- Other methods → `405` with `allow: GET, HEAD`.

`load` also returns `lastModified: number` (a millisecond timestamp).

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Compute the representation first, then the validators, then decide the status.
That ordering is what makes the 304 and the 200 agree by construction — they
are the same headers with one branch deciding whether the body and its
description go out.

## Hint 2

The precedence rule in code is a single `if`/`else if`, and the `else` is the
important half:

```ts
if (req.headers["if-none-match"] !== undefined) {
  notModified = matchesAny(...);
} else if (req.headers["if-modified-since"] !== undefined) {
  notModified = Math.floor(lastModified / 1000) <= parsedHeaderSeconds;
}
```

Evaluating both and combining them with `&&` or `||` is the bug: the entity tag
is authoritative when present, and the date is only a fallback for clients that
never received a tag.

## Hint 3

Second-truncation is the silent failure in this exercise. `Date.parse` on an
HTTP date gives you whole seconds; your stored `lastModified` almost certainly
has milliseconds. Comparing them directly makes the document look permanently
newer than the client's copy, so you return 200 forever and nobody notices,
because 200 is not an error. `Math.floor(lastModified / 1000)` on both sides.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the client does with each header on the 304. It already has
the body; what it is collecting is fresh *metadata* — a new `Cache-Control`
window, a confirmed `ETag`, the `Vary` it should key on. Omitting them means
the client's stored copy reverts to heuristic freshness, which is a guess based
on `Last-Modified`, and now you have a cache whose lifetime you do not control.

## Hint 2

`vary: accept-encoding` is on both responses on purpose. It tells any shared
cache that a gzipped variant and an identity variant are different stored
objects. Without it, a proxy that compresses can serve compressed bytes to a
client that never advertised support, and the failure looks like a corrupt
download rather than a caching bug.

## Hint 3

`private, max-age=60` is worth reading as a sentence: a browser may keep this
for a minute; a shared cache may not keep it at all. That combination is the
default for anything user-specific. Change `private` to `public` only when you
can state who else may see the bytes, and remember from the review that
`Authorization` on the request already blocks shared storage unless you
explicitly opt in.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — Cache-Control as data

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Export `parseCacheControl`, `buildCacheControl` and
`freshnessOf`.

`parseCacheControl(value)` → `Record<string, string | true>`: directive names
lowercased, valueless directives mapped to `true`, quoted values unquoted,
empty segments skipped, later duplicates ignored (first wins). A non-string
input gives `{}`.

`buildCacheControl(directives)` emits, in this order and only when present:
`public` / `private` / `no-store` / `no-cache`, `max-age`, `s-maxage`,
`must-revalidate`, `immutable`, `stale-while-revalidate`, `stale-if-error`.
Numeric directives must be non-negative integers or it is a `TypeError`.
`public` and `private` together is a `TypeError` — they contradict.

`freshnessOf(parsed, { shared })` returns the lifetime in seconds a cache of
that kind may use, applying the real precedence:

- `no-store` or `no-cache` → `0`;
- a shared cache prefers `s-maxage` over `max-age`; a private cache ignores
  `s-maxage` entirely;
- a shared cache must return `0` when `private` is present;
- no applicable directive → `null`, meaning "no explicit lifetime" — which is
  not the same as zero, because a cache may then apply a heuristic.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Parsing is a split-and-fold; the interesting work is `freshnessOf`, which is
where the directives stop being strings and become a policy. Write it as a
sequence of early returns in precedence order and it reads like the
specification: refuse first, then shared-specific, then general.

## Hint 2

The distinction between `0` and `null` is the subtlety worth care. `max-age=0`
means "this is stale immediately, revalidate" — the cache still stores it and
still asks. `null` means you said nothing, and a cache is then permitted to
invent a lifetime from `Last-Modified` (the common heuristic is a tenth of the
time since last modification). Conflating them means an endpoint you thought
was uncacheable gets cached for hours.

## Hint 3

`public` and `private` being mutually exclusive is a `TypeError` rather than a
last-wins because there is no defensible interpretation. Real caches disagree
about which to honour, so a response carrying both behaves differently in
different CDNs — the worst possible outcome for a directive whose entire job is
to say who may store your user's data.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Learn the four directives people confuse, in one breath: `no-store` means do
not write it down; `no-cache` means write it down but ask before every reuse;
`private` means only the user's own browser may write it down; `must-
revalidate` means once it is stale, never serve it without asking. Being able
to say those without hedging is most of what this exercise is teaching.

## Hint 2

`s-maxage` exists because the two audiences want different numbers. A CDN can
hold a product page for five minutes; a browser holding it for five minutes
means a user who edits it sees the old one. `max-age=0, s-maxage=300` is a
common and useful combination: always revalidate with the CDN, let the CDN
serve from its own copy.

## Hint 3

Think about the ordering in `buildCacheControl` as a readability decision, not
a protocol one — the directives are an unordered set as far as parsers are
concerned. A fixed order makes responses diffable and snapshot tests quiet,
which is the same argument as the key ordering in the problem-document builder
two sectors ago. Consistency is a feature even where the specification is
indifferent.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — the key a cache actually stores under

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Export `normalizeVary(header)` and
`cacheKey(request, varyHeader)`.

`normalizeVary(header)` → the field names a cache must include in its key:
lowercased, trimmed, de-duplicated, **sorted**, empties dropped. A header
containing `*` returns the string `"*"` on its own, whatever else is listed.

`cacheKey({ method, url, headers }, varyHeader)` → a string key, or `null` when
the response is not reusable (`Vary: *`, or a method other than `GET`/`HEAD`).

The key is built from:

- the method, uppercased (`HEAD` keys separately from `GET`);
- the URL with its query parameters **sorted by name, then by value**, so
  `?b=2&a=1` and `?a=1&b=2` share one entry;
- then one line per varied header, `name: value`, in sorted name order, where
  the value is the request's value with leading/trailing whitespace removed and
  internal runs of whitespace collapsed to one space;
- a header that is **absent** contributes `name: �` — a marker that cannot
  collide with any real value, because "absent" and "empty string" must not
  share a cache entry;
- `accept-encoding` is normalised further: split on commas, strip `;q=`
  parameters, lowercase, sort, re-join with `,`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A cache key is a function from a request to an identity, and every
normalisation you add is a claim that two requests deserve the same stored
response. Sorting query parameters is such a claim, and it is true for almost
every API — but it is a decision, not a fact, and it is worth being able to
name a case where it would be wrong (a signature computed over the raw query
string, for instance).

## Hint 2

The absent-versus-empty distinction is the trap. If a missing `accept-encoding`
and `accept-encoding: ` both key to `"accept-encoding: "`, then a client that
sent nothing can receive a response stored for a client that sent an empty
value — which in the encoding case means possibly-compressed bytes. Any
sentinel outside the printable range works; `�` is conventional because a
header value legally cannot contain it.

## Hint 3

Normalising `accept-encoding` beyond whitespace is what stops variant
explosion. Browsers send `gzip, deflate, br`, `br;q=1.0, gzip;q=0.8`,
`gzip,deflate` and a dozen other spellings that all mean the same thing to your
server. Without normalisation each is a separate stored object, and the hit
rate collapses for no reason. Real CDNs go further and normalise it to two
values — "supports brotli" and "does not" — which is the same idea taken to its
conclusion.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what happens when the key is too coarse and when it is too fine. Too coarse
is a correctness bug: a request receives a response built for a different one,
which is how a cache serves user A's page to user B. Too fine is a performance
bug: every request misses. `Vary: User-Agent` is the classic too-fine case —
millions of distinct values, so effectively no caching, with all of the storage
cost.

## Hint 2

`Vary: *` returning `"*"` and then a `null` key is the correct reading of the
specification: it means the response varies on something not expressible as a
header, so nothing may be reused. In practice it is a way of saying "do not
cache" that also survives an intermediary rewriting your `Cache-Control` — a
belt-and-braces move you will occasionally see in front of authenticated
endpoints.

## Hint 3

Note that the key does *not* include `Authorization` unless `Vary` names it —
and that this is why RFC 9111 has a separate rule making authorised responses
unstorable by shared caches by default. Two independent mechanisms guard the
same mistake, which tells you how often it was made. The review at the end of
this sector implements that second mechanism.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 5 — preconditions, in the order the specification says

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Export
`evaluatePreconditions(request, resource, options)`.

```ts
interface Request { method: string; headers: Record<string, string | undefined> }
interface Resource { exists: boolean; etag?: string; lastModified?: number }

type Verdict =
  | { kind: "proceed" }
  | { kind: "status"; status: 304 | 412 | 428 };
```

Implement RFC 9110 §13.2.2 exactly:

1. `if-match` present → strong comparison against `resource.etag`; `*` matches
   only when the resource exists. Failure is `412`. **If it is present, steps 2
   is skipped whatever the outcome.**
2. else `if-unmodified-since` present → failure (`lastModified` in whole
   seconds is *after* the header) is `412`.
3. `if-none-match` present → weak comparison; `*` matches when the resource
   exists. A **match** is a failure: `304` for `GET`/`HEAD`, `412` for anything
   else. If it is present, step 4 is skipped.
4. else, for `GET`/`HEAD` only, `if-modified-since` present → if the resource
   is not newer, `304`.
5. otherwise `{ kind: "proceed" }`.

`options.requireIfMatch` — when true and the method is unsafe (`PUT`, `PATCH`,
`DELETE`) and no `if-match` was sent — returns `428` **before** any of the
above.

Unparseable dates are ignored (treated as absent). `if-unmodified-since` and
`if-modified-since` are ignored for a resource with no `lastModified`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the five steps as five blocks in order, with the "else" relationships as
literal `else if`. The single most common bug in this algorithm is evaluating
step 2 after step 1 has already run — the specification says the date form is a
*fallback* for the tag form, not an additional condition, and combining them
lets a stale write through as a 304.

## Hint 2

Note the asymmetry in step 3 that surprises everyone: for a `GET`, a matching
`If-None-Match` means "you already have it" and earns a 304; for a `PUT`, the
same match means "the precondition you asked for is not satisfied" and earns a
412. Same header, same comparison, two statuses, decided by whether the method
is safe.

## Hint 3

The `428` is the strongest thing here and it is only three lines. Without it,
a client that forgets `If-Match` gets a successful unconditional write, and
lost updates are possible again; with it, the server has made them
*impossible*, because an unconditional write is refused with an explanation.
That is the difference between an API that supports optimistic concurrency and
one that requires it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the algorithm as protecting two different things. Steps 1 and 2 protect
the *resource*: do not let this write land if the world moved. Steps 3 and 4
protect the *client's bandwidth*: do not send bytes it already has. Ordering
the resource protection first is what stops a bandwidth optimisation from
silently discarding a write.

## Hint 2

`*` means different things by header and it is worth stating both. `If-Match:
*` succeeds when the resource exists — an update-only write. `If-None-Match: *`
succeeds when it does not — a create-only write, and the standard way to make
`PUT` behave like an atomic "create if absent" without a race between a `GET`
and a `PUT`.

## Hint 3

Ignoring unparseable dates rather than rejecting them is a rare place where
leniency is correct, and the reason is history: date parsing in the wild has
three legal formats and a long tail of broken clients. The specification says a
recipient that cannot parse a date must ignore the header. Treating it as an
error would fail requests for a condition the client cannot express — the
opposite of what the header is for.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Single-flight is the heart of this and it is five lines: keep a second map from
key to the *promise*, not the value. The first caller creates it, everyone else
finds it, and a `finally` deletes it. Storing only settled values is what
produces the thundering herd — a hundred callers all see "no value" at the same
instant and all call `load`.

## Hint 2

```ts
function refresh(key: string, load: () => Promise<V>): Promise<V> {
  const flight = inflight.get(key);
  if (flight !== undefined) return flight;
  const promise = load()
    .then((value) => { entries.set(key, { value, storedAt: now() }); return value; })
    .finally(() => inflight.delete(key));
  inflight.set(key, promise);
  return promise;
}
```

Note the `finally` rather than a `then`: the in-flight record must be cleared
on rejection too, or one failed load poisons the key until the process
restarts.

## Hint 3

For the background refresh, the returned promise must not be awaited by the
caller and its rejection must not become unhandled. `void refresh(key,
load).catch(() => {})` is the honest spelling: the caller already has a value
to return, and a failed background refresh is a metric, not an error for this
request. Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection terminates the process, so the
`.catch` is load-bearing rather than tidy.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Picture the failure this prevents. A popular key expires at second 60. Three
hundred requests arrive in the same millisecond. Without single-flight that is
three hundred simultaneous database queries; the database slows down, so the
loads take longer, so more requests pile up behind the same missing key. The
cache has amplified a routine expiry into an outage of the thing it was
protecting.

## Hint 2

`stale-while-revalidate` removes the cliff and single-flight removes the herd,
and they are different mechanisms for the same class of problem. With both, an
expiry costs exactly one background load and zero user-visible latency. This is
the same pair of ideas the HTTP header does at the CDN layer — you are
implementing in-process what a CDN does across the network.

## Hint 3

The LRU detail is small but worth doing properly: a `Map` in JavaScript
preserves insertion order, so "delete and re-set on use" moves an entry to the
end, and eviction is `entries.keys().next().value`. That is the whole LRU, and
knowing it means you rarely need a dependency for a bounded cache — though a
real one would also bound by *bytes*, since a thousand small entries and a
thousand large ones are not the same memory risk.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — the date format, and the second that disappears

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Export `formatHttpDate`, `parseHttpDate` and
`notModifiedSince`.

- `formatHttpDate(ms)` → the IMF-fixdate form,
  `Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT`, always GMT, always that spelling. A
  non-finite input is a `TypeError`.
- `parseHttpDate(value)` → milliseconds, or `null`. Accept all three formats a
  recipient must handle: IMF-fixdate, the obsolete RFC 850 form
  (`Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT`), and the asctime form
  (`Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 1994`). Two-digit years in the RFC 850 form map to
  1969–2068 by the usual rule. Anything else is `null`, never a throw.
- `notModifiedSince(lastModifiedMs, header)` → `true` when the resource has not
  changed since the client's copy: compare **whole seconds** on both sides,
  and treat an unparseable or absent header as `false`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new Date(ms).toUTCString()` produces IMF-fixdate exactly, including the
two-digit day and the `GMT` suffix — so the formatter is one line plus a
validity check. Resist building it from parts; the format has a fixed-width day
field that hand-rolled versions get wrong for the first nine days of a month,
and that bug only appears for a few days each month.

## Hint 2

Second-truncation is the silent bug this exercise exists for:

```ts
Math.floor(lastModifiedMs / 1000) <= Math.floor(parsed / 1000)
```

A stored `12:00:00.500` compared against a header of `12:00:00` reads as newer,
so you answer 200 forever, the client re-downloads every time, and nothing ever
errors. Floor both sides. This is also why `Last-Modified` is a *weak*
validator: two changes within one second are indistinguishable.

## Hint 3

For the two obsolete formats, convert them to something `Date.parse` handles
rather than writing a parser: a regex that pulls the fields out, then
`Date.UTC(...)`. The two-digit year rule (`>= 70` means 19xx) is inherited from
RFC 2822 and is why the obsolete format was deprecated in the first place.
Supporting it is a two-line branch and it is required of a recipient — the
strictness you can afford is on what you *emit*.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The general principle here is worth more than the format: be strict in what you
send, lenient in the specific ways the specification requires you to be when
receiving. That is not Postel's law in its discredited general form — it is a
narrow, enumerated list of three formats, which is exactly what makes it safe.
Lenient parsing is dangerous when the set of accepted inputs is open-ended, not
when it is written down.

## Hint 2

Why `Last-Modified` still exists alongside ETags: it is derivable from
filesystem metadata with no read of the content, it is human-readable in a log,
and it enables `If-Range` fallbacks. Its weakness — one-second resolution — is
also why a system that writes twice a second cannot rely on it. Use both when
you can: the tag decides, the date is a fallback for clients that never got a
tag.

## Hint 3

Returning `null` rather than throwing from `parseHttpDate` is a contract that
propagates outward: RFC 9110 requires a recipient that cannot parse a date to
*ignore the header*. Throwing would turn a client's bad clock string into a 500
on your side, which is both wrong and a free denial of service. Fail soft on
input you must tolerate; fail hard on your own mistakes, which is why the
formatter throws.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — writes, and invalidation you cannot forget

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Export `createVersionedStore()` returning
`{ read, write, remove, collectionEtag, size }`.

Every item has a value and a version. The ETag of an item is
`"<id>-<version>"`; the ETag of the collection is a **strong** tag over a
canonical listing of `id:version` pairs sorted by id, so that any write changes
it automatically.

- `read(id)` → `{ value, etag, version } | null`.
- `write(id, value, ifMatch)`:
  - the item does not exist and `ifMatch` is absent or `*` → create, version 1,
    `{ status: 201, etag }`;
  - the item does not exist and `ifMatch` names a tag → `{ status: 412 }`;
  - the item exists and `ifMatch` is absent → `{ status: 428 }`;
  - the item exists and `ifMatch` is `*` or matches the current tag
    (**strong** comparison) → update, version + 1, `{ status: 200, etag }`;
  - otherwise → `{ status: 412 }` and **no change**.
- `remove(id, ifMatch)` follows the same precondition rules and answers
  `{ status: 204 }` or `{ status: 404 }` / `{ status: 412 }` / `{ status: 428 }`.
- `collectionEtag()` must differ before and after any successful write or
  removal, and must be identical for two stores holding the same items
  regardless of insertion order.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The design idea is that invalidation should be *structural*, not remembered. If
the collection's validator is a hash over the ids and versions, then a write
changes a version, which changes the hash, and no code anywhere has to call an
`invalidate()`. Caches whose correctness depends on someone remembering to
purge are the ones that are wrong six months later.

## Hint 2

Sorting by id before hashing is what makes the tag *canonical*: two stores that
received the same writes in different orders must produce the same tag, or a
cache in front of two replicas will thrash between two validators for identical
content. Canonicalisation before hashing is the same discipline as in
signatures and Merkle trees.

## Hint 3

The `428` case is the one that turns this from bookkeeping into a policy. An
existing item with no `If-Match` is an unconditional overwrite, which is a lost
update waiting to happen, so the store refuses it. A *creating* write is
different — there is nothing to lose — which is why an absent `If-Match` is
allowed there. Two branches, one for each, and the difference is the whole
argument for `428`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Version-based tags versus content hashes is a real trade. A version is cheap
(no hashing, no need to have the bytes) and changes even when the content did
not — a no-op update bumps it and invalidates caches unnecessarily. A content
hash is exact but requires the serialised body. Items here use versions because
a store knows them for free; the collection uses a hash because it is derived
from many items and you want it stable.

## Hint 2

Note that `write` returning `201` versus `200` matters to clients and to
caches: 201 means a new resource exists at a location, and a cache holding a
404 for that URL must drop it. This is the "invalidation by unsafe method" rule
in RFC 9111 — a successful `PUT`, `POST`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` invalidates the
cached response for the request URI. Your store models it structurally; a real
HTTP cache does it by watching the method.

## Hint 3

Strong comparison for `If-Match` is required, and here it is trivially
satisfied because your tags are never weak. Keep the comparison strict anyway:
the day someone adds a weak collection tag as an optimisation, a lenient
`If-Match` silently starts accepting writes based on "probably the same
version", which is exactly the guarantee the header exists to provide.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a caching layer in front of a slow origin

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. `createCachingHandler({ origin, now, ttlMs,
staleMs })` returns a `node:http` handler that sits in front of an injected
`origin(pathname, headers)` returning
`{ status, body: Buffer, contentType, etag, lastModified }` — and takes as long
as the gate wants it to.

- `GET` and `HEAD` are cacheable; every other method passes through to the
  origin and, on a `2xx`, **invalidates** the cached entries for that path.
- The cache key is the pathname with sorted query parameters, plus the
  `accept-encoding` request header normalised as in ex4, because responses
  carry `vary: accept-encoding`.
- A **fresh** entry is served without touching the origin, with
  `x-cache: HIT`. A **stale** entry (within `ttlMs + staleMs`) is served with
  `x-cache: STALE` and triggers one background refresh. A miss is
  `x-cache: MISS`.
- Concurrent misses for one key produce exactly **one** `origin` call.
- Every served response carries `etag`, `last-modified`, `vary:
  accept-encoding`, `cache-control: public, max-age=<ttl seconds>,
  stale-while-revalidate=<stale seconds>`, an exact `content-length`, and
  `age: <seconds since stored>` — `0` on a miss.
- A conditional request whose `if-none-match` matches the entry's `etag` gets
  `304` with the validators and no body, whether the entry was a hit, stale or
  a fresh miss.
- `HEAD` gets the `GET` headers and no body.
- An origin rejection with a stale entry available serves the stale copy with
  `x-cache: STALE-ERROR`; with nothing cached, it is a `502` with
  `{"error":"origin_failed"}`.

```
uv run dojo test node v3nb05_caching_etags challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Separate the cache from the HTTP. One function turns a request into a key and
a verdict; one store answers `get(key, load)` with the single-flight and
stale-while-revalidate logic from ex6; one function writes the response. If the
store knows what a `ServerResponse` is, you will not be able to test the
interesting behaviour without a socket.

## Hint 2

Order matters at the top of the handler: compute the key, then get the entry,
*then* evaluate the conditional request against the entry's ETag. Evaluating
`if-none-match` before you know which entry applies means comparing the
client's tag against whatever happened to be cached under a different variant —
which is a 304 for a body the client has never seen.

## Hint 3

`Age` is the header people omit and it is required for correctness in a chain
of caches: it tells the next cache down how much of the freshness lifetime has
already been consumed. Without it, each cache in the chain restarts the clock
and a `max-age=60` response can survive for minutes. It is
`Math.floor((now() - storedAt) / 1000)`, and `0` on a fresh fetch.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The invalidation-on-write rule is worth implementing deliberately rather than
as an afterthought. RFC 9111 says a successful unsafe method invalidates the
cached response for that URI, and the reason is immediate: a client that
`PUT`s and then `GET`s should not receive the version it just replaced. Because
your keys include the encoding variant, "invalidate the path" means dropping
every key with that pathname prefix — which is an argument for storing the
pathname alongside the entry rather than parsing it back out of the key.

## Hint 2

Think about what `x-cache` is for. It is not part of any specification; it is a
debugging convention that every CDN implements because the alternative is
guessing. Emitting it makes the gate's assertions possible and, more
importantly, makes a production cache observable — "is this endpoint even being
cached?" is otherwise a question you cannot answer from outside.

## Hint 3

Two edge cases the gate will find:

- a background refresh that rejects must not produce an unhandled rejection —
  the request that triggered it has already answered, and since Node 15 an
  unhandled rejection ends the process;
- a `HEAD` must not populate a cache entry that a later `GET` then serves as a
  body-less response. Key them separately or store the body regardless of the
  method that fetched it; the second is what real caches do, and it is why
  `HEAD` and `GET` share a key there.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is a sequence of guard clauses, and the order is the specification's own.
Write them as nine early returns and resist collapsing any pair into a single
condition — the reasons are the useful output, and a merged branch cannot say
which rule fired.

## Hint 2

Rule 6 is the one to understand rather than memorise. A response to an
authorised request is presumed to be about that user, so a shared cache must
not keep it. The exceptions are the response *explicitly* saying otherwise:
`public` (anyone may store this), `s-maxage` (here is a shared-cache lifetime,
so obviously shared caches are in scope), or `must-revalidate` (store it but
never serve it stale without checking). Together they are the API author saying
"I have thought about this".

## Hint 3

Rule 7's escape hatch is what makes a `301` or a `410` cacheable without a
`Cache-Control` at all — they are in the default set — while, say, a `500`
becomes cacheable only if you explicitly say so. Explicit freshness lets you
opt a status in; nothing lets you opt one out except `no-store`, which is why
that check comes first.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The value of writing this out is that it makes visible how much of "caching"
happens without your involvement. A response with a validator and no
`Cache-Control` is storable and gets a *heuristic* freshness lifetime — often a
tenth of the time since `Last-Modified` — chosen by someone else's cache. If
that surprises you, then every endpoint you have shipped with no cache headers
has been making a decision you did not know you were making.

## Hint 2

Notice the two independent mechanisms protecting authorised responses: this
rule, and `Vary` keying from ex4. Belt and braces exists here because the
consequence — one user's data served to another — is the worst outcome in the
whole sector, and because the mistake is easy: the endpoint works perfectly
until the day a CDN is put in front of it.

## Hint 3

A good interview follow-up to have an answer for: "what would you set on an
endpoint that returns a user's own profile?" — `private, no-store` if it is
sensitive, or `private, max-age=0, must-revalidate` with an ETag if you want
conditional requests to save bandwidth while guaranteeing freshness. Being able
to give the second answer, and to say why the ETag makes it cheap, is the whole
sector in one sentence.
